{{efn|name=Palmisano definitions 2010
|{{harvnb|Palmisano|Totaro|2010|p=519}}: "The absence of a common language is one of the reasons why nowadays there is a very big gap between the Architect and the Engineer. The introduction of new materials and techniques during the Industrial Revolution and the born of the first polytechnics in the 18th century, led to a different cultural approach to the design causing the born of different languages between Architects and Engineers. Nowadays, with the widespread of very complicated works of the architecture there is a huge need to bridge the gap between Architects and Engineers. In this context, focusing the attention on masonry domes, this paper aims at highlighting that Load Path Method seems to open new prospects in the search for a common language between engineers and architects to give voice, in harmony and in a single design, to formal, aesthetical, functional and structural aspects. According to LPM, a dome can be seen as a system of meridian arches joined by the parallel circles. The arches draw the paths of the vertical loads while the parallel circles draw the paths of the unbalanced thrusts. In fact, differently from the arches, in dome the equilibrium of the thrusts in every node is always possible because of the presence of the parallels."
}}

{{efn|name=Clarke definitions 2010
|{{harvnb|Clarke|2010|p=79}}: "dome A vault of even curvature over a circular base; the section can be segmental, semicircular, pointed, or bulbous. If a vault is erected over a square base, squinches or pendentives must be inserted at the corners to connect the dome to the base."
}}

{{efn|name=Ching definitions 2011
|{{harvnb|Ching|2011|p=62}}: "A vaulted structure having a circular plan and usually the form of a portion of a sphere, so constructed as to exert an equal thrust in all directions."
}}

{{efn|name=Parker definitions 2012a
|{{harvnb|Parker|2012|p=97}}: "Dome, a cupola; the term is derived from the Italian duomo, a cathedral, the custom of erecting cupolas on those buildings having been so prevalent that the name dome has, in the French and English languages, been transferred from the church to this kind of roof [See Cupola.]"
}}

{{efn|name=Parker definitions 2012b
|{{harvnb|Parker|2012|p=90}}: "Cupola (Ital.), a concave ceiling, either hemispherical or of any other curve, covering a circular or polygonal area; also a roof, the exterior of which is either one of these forms, usually called a dome, and in Latin tholus."
}}

{{efn|name=Burden definitions 2012
|{{harvnb|Burden|2012|p=155}}: "Dome: a curved roof structure that spans an area on a circular base, producing an equal thrust in all directions. A cross section of the dome can be semicircular, pointed, or segmented."
}}

{{efn|name=Gorse definitions 2012
|{{harvnb|Gorse|Johnston|Pritchard|2012|p=115}}: "dome 1. A structure that has a hemispherical roof. 2. A curved layer of rock strata, formed by an upward fold."
}}

{{efn|name=Brett definitions 2012
|{{harvnb|Brett|2012|p=20}}: "Dome a vaulted roof; normally circular or polygonal in plan and semicircular, segmental or pointed in section. See also Cupola and Squinch."
}}

{{efn|name=Davies definitions 2012
|{{harvnb|Davies|Jokiniemi|2012|p=143}}: "Dome 1 a hollow, flattened or raised hemispherical roof structure, often of masonry, which rests on a circular, square, or polygonal base. See Types included as separate entries are listed below: bulbous dome, see onion dome; drum dome; half dome; melon dome, see umbrella dome; onion dome; parachute dome, see umbrella dome; pendentive dome; pumpkin dome, see umbrella dome; sail dome, sail vault; saucer dome; semi dome, see half dome; umbrella dome. 2 see domelight."
}}

{{efn|name=Hourihane definitions 2012
|{{harvnb|Hourihane|2012|p=301}}: "Rounded vault covering an interior space. A very small dome roof, for example a lantern mounted on the eye of a dome proper (e.g. St Paul's Cathedral, London), is known as a cupola. In Italian cupola is used for a monumental dome." [...] "A dome can either be composed of curved segments or be a shell of revolution. The dome at Florence Cathedral by Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446) is segmental, octangular at every section. A shell of revolution is generated by rotating an arch about a vertical central axis. To produce a hemispherical surface the arch will be semicircular, but and shape of arch, similarly rotated, will give rise to a shell of revolution; and every horizontal cross-section is still circular. The simplest form of dome is that of such a shell of revolution: for example, the inner masonry dome of St Paul's Cathedral is roughly hemispherical, and has an open eye, while the main dome is conical; but both are shells of revolution, as is the surface of the timber outer dome. A dome can have either a single or a double shell."
}}

{{efn|name=Harris definitions 2013
|{{harvnb|Harris|2013}}: "Dome 1. A curved roof structure spanning an area; often hemispherical in shape. 2. A vault substantially hemispherical in shape, but sometimes slightly pointed or bulbous; a ceiling of similar form."
}}

{{efn|name=Murray definitions 2013
|{{harvnb|Murray|Murray|Jones|2013|p=151}}: "dome A structure that can be either circular in plan, or oval, hexagonal, octagonal, or a combination of these forms. It may have a high profile, or hemispherical, or flattened."
}}

{{efn|name=Curl definitions 2015
|{{harvnb|Curl|Wilson|2015|pp=236–237}}: "Cupola, essentially a species of vault, constructed on a circular, elliptical, or polygonal plan, bulbous, segmental, semicircular, or pointed in vertical section. It can be built on top of a structure the plan of which is identical to that of the dome: if that structure's wall is circular or elliptical it is a drum (often pierced with windows) as in a rotunda. However, domes usually provide cover for a square- or rectangular-planned building or compartment, so adjustments are made to facilitate the transition from the square to the circular, elliptical, or polygonal base of the cupola or dome. This is achieved by means of pendentives (fragments of a sail-vault, resembling a species of concave, distorted, almost triangular spandrels, rising up from the corner at the top of the right-angled compartment to the circular or elliptical base of the drum or cupola) or squinches (small arch or series of parallel arches of increasing radius spanning the angle of the square compartment). Both the drum and cupola will have a diameter the same dimension as the side of the square on which the whole structure stands. Types of dome include: calotte: low cupola or saucer dome of segmental vertical section, like a skull-cap; cloister-vault: as domical vault; domical vault: cloister-vault, not a true dome, but formed of four or more (depending on the shape of the base) cells or webs forming groins where they touch vertically and rising to a point; melon: as parachute; Pantheon: low dome on the exterior, often stepped, resembling that of the Pantheon in Rome, and coffered on the interior, widely copied by Neo-Classical architects; parachute: melon, pumpkin, or umbrella dome standing on a scalloped circular base and formed of individual webs, segmental on plan, joined on groins or ribs. Each web has a concave interior and convex exterior so it resembles a parachute, rather than an umbrella; pumpkin: as parachute; sail dome: dome resembling a billowing sail over a square compartment with its diameter the same dimension as the diagonal instead of the side of the square below, enabling the structure to rise as though on pendentives but continuing without interruption. Pendentives are really part of a sail-dome and themselves are a species of sail-vault; umbrella: as parachute."
}}

{{efn|name=Palmer definitions 2016
|{{harvnb|Palmer|2016|p=123}}: "The dome, which is created from an arch turned on its axis 360 degrees, is traditionally considered one of the most important Ancient Roman architectural inventions."
}}

{{efn|name=Guedes definitions 2016
|{{harvnb|Guedes|2016|p=174}}: "The dome may be regarded as the three-dimensional counterpart of the arch. In its true circular form, a vertical arch is rotated around a vertical axis and sweeps out, at every level, a continuous circular horizontal ring. Loads can be transmitted both along the meridian lines of the vertical arches and around the horizontal rings."
}}

{{efn|name=Jannasch definitions 2016
|{{harvnb|Jannasch|2016|pp=745–746}}: "A funicular masonry dome experiences no hoop stresses, whether tensile or compressive, so it is always on the verge of bursting. Shallow spheric domes maintain compressive stresses in each course and are therefore more stable than the "ideal" funicular form. Viable non-funicular domes also include Herrero's flat vault at the Escorial, and Mackenzie's 1840 concept of an inverted fan vault." [...] "Masonry domes are often explained as free-standing arches rotated around a central axis, or as half-arches swept between a tension ring at the base and an ocular compression ring at the top. Such concepts aren't entirely inaccurate, but they are far from complete. They undervalue or ignore the circumferential compression in each course upon which the rising dome depends and which remains active in many completed structures. They also tend to ignore the vertical shear resistance that prevents inner and upper portions of the dome from crashing vertically down through outer and lower portions, and the horizontal shear resistance that allows lower parts of the dome to contain the thrust of upper parts. Visualizing the dome as a rotated arch implies that the bedding faces between subsequent courses of masonry need to be more or less normal to the section, which is the case in an arch, but not the case in a dome. Lastly, free-standing arches must be thick enough to contain their funicular. This is not true of domes. That the arch and funicular don't really explain of the structural behavior of domes should be clear from real world examples. The conical domes at Pisa and elsewhere, for example, the shallow domes of Byzantium, and the circular vaults at the Escorial are far from funicular. None of them would succeed if "un-rotated" into arches."
}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Early skyscrapers
======================================================================

{{short description|Tall commercial buildings built between 1884 and 1945}}
[[File:Detroit Photographic Company (0645).jpg|thumb|The [[Flatiron Building]], [[New York City]], shortly after its construction in 1903|alt=A wedge-shaped Italianate-designed building seen head-on at the angle]]

The earliest stage of [[skyscraper]] design encompasses buildings built between 1884 and 1945, predominantly in American cities, especially [[New York City|New York]] and [[Chicago]]. Cities in the United States were traditionally made up of [[low-rise]] buildings, but significant economic growth after the [[American Civil War]] and increasingly intensive use of urban land encouraged the development of taller buildings beginning in the 1870s. Technological improvements enabled the construction of [[Fireproofing|fireproofed]] iron-framed structures with [[deep foundation]]s, equipped with new inventions such as the [[elevator]] and [[electric lighting]]. These made it both technically and commercially viable to build a new class of taller buildings, the first of which, Chicago's {{convert|138|ft|adj=on}} tall [[Home Insurance Building]], opened in 1885. Their numbers grew rapidly, and by 1888 they were being labelled "skyscrapers".

Chicago initially led the way in skyscraper design, with many constructed in the center of its financial district during the late 1880s and early 1890s. Sometimes termed the products of the [[Chicago school (architecture)|Chicago school of architecture]], these skyscrapers attempted to balance aesthetic concerns with practical commercial design, producing large, square ''[[palazzo]]''-styled buildings hosting shops and restaurants on the ground level and containing rentable offices on the upper floors. In contrast, New York's skyscrapers were frequently narrower towers which, more eclectic in style, were often criticized for their lack of elegance. In 1892, Chicago banned the construction of new skyscrapers taller than {{convert|150|ft}}, leaving the development of taller buildings to New York.

A new wave of skyscraper construction emerged in the first decade of the 20th century. The demand for new office space to hold the expanding workforce of [[White-collar worker|white-collar staff]] in the U.S. continued to grow. Engineering developments made it easier to build and live in yet taller buildings. Chicago built new skyscrapers in its existing style, while New York experimented further with tower design. Iconic buildings such as the [[Flatiron Building|Flatiron]] were followed by the {{convert|612|ft|adj=on}} tall [[Singer Tower]], the {{convert|700|ft|adj=on}} [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower]], and the {{convert|792|ft|adj=on}} [[Woolworth Building]]. Though these skyscrapers were commercial successes, criticism mounted as they broke up the ordered city skyline and plunged neighboring streets and buildings into perpetual shadow. Combined with an economic downturn, this led to the [[1916 Zoning Resolution|introduction of zoning restraints]] in New York in 1916.

In the [[Interwar period|interwar years]], skyscrapers spread to nearly all major U.S. cities, while a total of around 100 were built in some other Western countries (like Argentina, Brazil, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, United Kingdom etc.) and Asian countries (China, Japan). The [[Roaring Twenties|economic boom of the 1920s]] and extensive real estate speculation encouraged a wave of new skyscraper projects in New York and Chicago. New York City's 1916 Zoning Resolution helped shape the [[Art Deco]] or "[[Setback (architecture)|set-back]]" style of skyscrapers, leading to structures that focused on volume and striking silhouettes, often richly decorated. Skyscraper heights continued to grow, with the [[Chrysler Building|Chrysler]] and the [[Empire State Building]]s each claiming new records, reaching {{convert|1,046|ft}} and {{convert|1,250|ft}} respectively. With the onset of the [[Great Depression]], the real estate market collapsed, and new construction stuttered to a halt, ending this era of skyscraper construction. Popular and academic culture embraced the skyscraper through films, photography, literature, and ballet, seeing the buildings as either positive symbols of modernity and science, or alternatively examples of the ills of modern life and society. Skyscraper projects after [[World War II]] typically rejected the designs of the early skyscrapers, instead embracing the [[International style (architecture)|international]] style; many older skyscrapers were redesigned to suit contemporary tastes or even demolished—such as the Singer Tower, once the world's tallest skyscraper.

==Background: 1850–1879==
===Skyscraper precursors===
{{Main|List of tallest buildings and structures#History}}
Tall structures have been built in some form or another for millennia. Egypt's [[Great Pyramid of Giza]], built in the 26th century BC at a height of {{convert|481|feet}},{{refn|It has since weathered down to {{convert|454.4|feet}}.|group=nb}}<ref>{{harvnb|Stanborough|2016|p=26}}</ref> would remain the tallest structure on Earth for millennia until it was surpassed in the Middle Ages.{{refn|The title is usually said to have passed to [[Lincoln Cathedral]] in England at a height of {{convert|525|feet}} in 1311,<ref>{{harvnb|Porter|Prince|2010|p=588}}</ref> although others dispute this figure.<ref name="Kendrick 1902 60">{{cite book|last=Kendrick|first=A. F.|title=The Cathedral Church of Lincoln: A History and Description of its Fabric and a List of the Bishops|url=https://archive.org/details/cathedralchurcho00kend|year=1902|publisher=George Bell & Sons|location=London|isbn=978-1-178-03666-4|page=[https://archive.org/details/cathedralchurcho00kend/page/60 60]|chapter=2: The Central Tower|quote=The tall spire of timber, covered with lead, which originally crowned this tower reached an altitude, it is said, of 525 feet; but this is doubtful. This spire was blown down during a tempest in January 1547–8.}}</ref>|group=nb}} The term "skyscraper" was first used in the 1780s to describe a particularly tall horse, before later being applied to, among other things, the [[skysail|sail at the top of a ship's mast]], tall hats and bonnets, tall men, and a ball that was hit high into the air.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=ix}}</ref> In the 1880s it began to be applied to buildings, first in 1883 to describe large public monuments and then in 1889 as a label for tall office blocks, coming into widespread use over the next decade.<ref name="Landau 1996 ix–x">{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=ix–x}}; {{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=115}}</ref>

Unlike the tall buildings of Antiquity and the Middle Ages, which were primarily built for ceremonial and religious purposes, skyscrapers were largely targeted towards business applications.<ref name="Landau 1996 ix–x"/> Various [[#Technological developments|technological developments]] of the 19th century, which included such design elements as [[wind bracing]] and crucially the use of an [[Steel frame|iron-framed skeleton]], further differentiated skyscrapers from earlier tall secular buildings, such as those in [[Old Town, Edinburgh|the Old Town of Edinburgh]].<ref name="Edinburgh">{{cite web |title=Old and New Towns of Edinburgh |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/728 |website=World Heritage Conservation |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=24 January 2023 |location=Paris}}</ref>

Development of these skyscrapers was concentrated in the American cities of [[New York City|New York]] and [[Chicago]], but was not entirely exclusive to them; precursors of the form exist in Europe, especially the United Kingdom. The [[Ditherington Flax Mill]] was built in [[Shropshire]] in 1797 as the world's first iron-framed building, and as such has been referred to as "the father of the skyscraper".<ref name="Ditherington">{{cite web |title='Father of the skyscraper' rescued for the nation |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/server/show/ConWebDoc.4839 |publisher=English Heritage |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060213213221/https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/server/show/ConWebDoc.4839 |archive-date=February 13, 2006}}</ref>

===Commercial and social drivers===
Early skyscrapers emerged in the United States as a result of economic growth, the financial organization of American businesses, and the intensive use of land.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=114}}</ref> New York City was one of the centers of early skyscraper construction and had a history as a key seaport located on the small island of [[Manhattan]], on the east coast of the U.S.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=135}}</ref> As a consequence of its colonial history and [[Commissioners' Plan of 1811|city planning]], New York's real estate was broken up into many small parcels of land, with few large sites.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=36}}</ref> During the first half of the 19th century it became the national center of American finance, and the banks in the [[Financial District, Manhattan|financial district of Manhattan]] competed fiercely with English institutions for international dominance.<ref>{{harvnb|Severini|1983|p=55}}</ref>

The [[Great Fire of New York|Great Fire of 1835]] destroyed most of the old financial buildings, and in their place a wide variety of new buildings were erected and demolished in quick succession during the 1840s and 1850s; traveler Philip Hone suggested that the entire city was being rebuilt every decade.<ref>{{harvnb|Severini|1983|pp=39–40, 79}}; {{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=24}}</ref> Most buildings adopted the [[Renaissance architecture|Italian Renaissance]] inspired ''[[Palazzo style architecture|palazzo]]''-style of architecture popular in England, and rose no more than five or six stories.<ref>{{harvnb|Severini|1983|p=57}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=10}}</ref> New York did not have any [[Height restriction laws|restrictions on the height]] of buildings, but in practice low-rise buildings were the norm, at least until 1865, with the tallest buildings being the city's churches.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=34}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=4}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=20}}</ref> New York's population tripled between 1840 and 1870, and property values soared, increasing by more than 90 percent between 1860 and 1875.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=1–2}}</ref>

[[File:Downtown Chicago, 1874.jpg|thumb|left|[[Currier and Ives]]' 1874 map of Chicago shows low-rise buildings constructed after the [[Great Chicago Fire|fire of 1871]]|alt=A drawing of many square four- to five-story buildings, flatly covered]]

Further west, the city of Chicago became the other major site in the development of early skyscrapers. In contrast to New York, Chicago emerged as a major metropolis only in the mid-19th century, growing from a village of {{nowrap|around fifty inhabitants in 1830}}, {{nowrap|to a city of 30,000 in 1850}} and {{nowrap|nearly 300,000 by 1870}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=3}}</ref> Chicago became the railroad hub for the [[Western United States|American West]] and the primary trading city for the emerging territories, famous for its commercial culture.<ref>{{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=68}}; {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=1}}</ref> It saw itself as different from the cities on the east coast and was immensely proud of its status as a growing, vibrant center.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=121}}</ref> As early as 1868, its commercial buildings were touted as being "unequalled in the East for grandeur, business, or wealth", but such claims were regarded as risible.{{refn|William Corkran, arriving from New York that year to become the librarian of the [[Chicago Historical Society]], noted that "Driving slowly down [[Lake Street (Chicago)|Lake Street]], which was then the principal street, he [a representative from the Society] pointed out some three or four stores, which he assured me were unequalled in the East for grandeur, business, or wealth. We could not help an involuntary smile at the impertinence [impudence] of the assertion, as we believed we could find as good stores on [[Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)|Tenth]], or even [[Eleventh Avenue (Manhattan)|Eleventh Avenue]]."<ref>{{harvnb|Angle|1956|p=40}}</ref>|group=nb}}

By the 1870s, Chicago had become the main financial center for the West, but in October 1871 the [[Great Chicago Fire]] destroyed the majority of the wooden structures within the city.<ref>{{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=345}}; {{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=5}}; {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=112}}</ref> The city was rebuilt on large plots of land in a [[grid plan|grid network]]<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=36}}; {{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=346}}</ref> and followed new city ordinances that prohibited construction in wood.<ref>{{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=346}}; {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=114}}</ref> These factors encouraged the building of taller properties in new innovative designs, which, like New York, saw a range of businesses and services being packed into single buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=346}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=35}}</ref> Especially popular in the post-fire era were "commercial blocks", several-story masonry buildings built to property lines with only one street facade that was adorned in such styles as Italianate, Classical Revival, and English Gothic. Such blocks, which were very flexible in their use, had already been prolific before the fire, and early post-fire reconstruction differed from the old styles downtown only in scale.<ref>{{harvnb|Holden Block Report|2011|p=5}}</ref>

The construction of taller buildings during the&nbsp;1870s was hindered by the financial [[Panic of 1873]] and the ensuing economic depression, which lasted until around&nbsp;1879.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=18}}</ref> Construction slowed, and property values slumped.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=18, 109}}</ref> By 1880, however, the recovery was well underway, with new construction in New York returning to the pace of 1871,<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=109}}</ref> and the economic upturn making the construction of taller buildings an attractive financial option again, establishing many of the preconditions for the development of the skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=114–115}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=18}}</ref>

===Technological developments===
{{main|Skyscraper design and construction}}
[[File:Structural design of the NY Produce Exchange.jpg|thumb|The [[2 Broadway|Produce Exchange]] of 1884 made structural advances in metal frame design|alt=A cross-sectional drawing of several floors]]

The emergence of skyscrapers was made possible by technological improvements during the middle of the 19th century.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=5}}</ref> One of these developments was the iron framed building. Masonry buildings supported their internal floors through their walls, but the taller the building, the thicker the walls had to become, particularly at the base.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=116–117}}</ref> In the 1860s, French engineers experimented with using built-up [[plate girder]]s made of [[wrought iron]] to construct buildings supported by internal metal frames.<ref name=LandauConditPP21>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=21–22}}</ref> These frames were stronger than traditional masonry and permitted much thinner walls.<ref name=LandauConditPP21/> The methodology was extensively described in engineering journals and was initially used to build warehouses.<ref name=LandauConditPP21/>

Using these metal frames for taller buildings, however, meant exposing them to increased [[wind engineering|wind pressure]].<ref name=LandauConditP23>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=23}}</ref> As a consequence, protective [[wind bracing]] had to be introduced, enabled by the work of [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]] who produced equations for calculating the [[Structural load|loads]] and [[Moment (physics)|moments]] on larger buildings.<ref name=LandauConditP23/>{{refn|Despite this work on wind pressure, up until the late 1890s it was still, incorrectly, believed that wide skyscrapers did not need wind bracing.<ref name="Condit 1968 125">{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=125}}</ref>|group=nb}} Metal-framed buildings were also vulnerable to fire and required special [[fireproofing]].<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=116}}</ref> French engineers had made advances in this area in the early 19th century, and major breakthroughs came with the work of architect [[Peter Bonnett Wight|Peter Wight]] in the 1860s.<ref name=LandauConditP24>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=24}}</ref> Spurred on by the catastrophic fires in Chicago in 1871 and [[Great Boston Fire of 1872|Boston in 1872]], his findings were turned into a wide variety of patented fireproofing products during the 1870s.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=27–30}}</ref>

Taller, heavier buildings such as skyscrapers also required stronger foundations than smaller buildings. Earlier buildings had typically rested their foundations on rubble, which was in turn laid down on the soft top layer of the ground called the [[overburden]].<ref name=LandauConditPP23>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=23–24}}</ref> As buildings became taller and heavier, the overburden could not support their weight, and foundations increasingly needed to rest directly on the [[bedrock]] below.<ref name=LandauConditPP23/> In both New York and Chicago this required digging down a considerable distance through soft soil and often below the [[water table]], risking the hole filling up with water before the foundations were complete. The deeper the foundations needed to be, the greater the challenge.<ref name=LandauConditP24/> Special water-tight boxes called [[Caisson (engineering)|caissons]] were invented to deal with this problem in England in 1830 and adopted in the U.S. during the 1850s and 1860s.<ref name=LandauConditP24/>

[[File:Caissons, 1898.jpg|thumb|left|Early skyscraper [[Caisson (engineering)|caisson]] foundations, 1898|alt=An engineering drawing of subterranean "piers", or caissons]]

The development of the [[elevator]] was also essential to the emergence of the early skyscrapers, as office buildings taller than around six stories would have been impractical without them.<ref name=LandauConditP35>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=35}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=84}}</ref> Powered elevators were first installed in England during the 1830s and spread to U.S. factories and hotels by the 1840s.<ref name=LandauConditP35/> Elevators using hoist ropes, however, could only function effectively in low-rise buildings, and this limitation encouraged the introduction of the hydraulic elevator in 1870, even though early models contained dangerous design flaws.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=36}}</ref> By 1876 these problems had been resolved, providing a solution for servicing the early skyscrapers.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=36–37}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=21}}</ref>

New environmental technologies in heating, lighting, [[Ventilation (architecture)|ventilation]] and sanitation were also critical to creating taller buildings that were attractive to work in. [[Central heating]] could not be easily extended to serve larger buildings;<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=30–31}}</ref> in the 1850s, a system using low-pressure steam and steam-operated fans became adopted in the construction of the later skyscrapers.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=30}}</ref> Many U.S. buildings were [[gas light|lit by gas]], but this carried safety risks and was difficult to install in taller buildings.<ref name=LandauConditP38>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=38}}</ref> As an alternative, [[electric light]]s were installed from 1878 onwards, powered by basement generators.<ref name=LandauConditP38/> Ventilation was also a challenge, as smoke drifting into offices from the streets and the fumes from the gas lighting made [[Indoor air quality|air quality]] a major health issue.<ref name=LandauConditP32>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=32}}</ref> A steam-driven, forced-draft ventilation system was invented in 1860 and became widely used in taller buildings by the 1870s, overcoming much of the problem.<ref name=LandauConditP32/> Improvements in iron piping permitted running hot and cold water and sanitation facilities to be installed throughout taller buildings for the first time.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=33–34}}</ref>

==Emergence of the skyscraper: 1880–1899==

===The first skyscraper===
[[File:Home Insurance Building.JPG|thumb|Chicago's [[Home Insurance Building]], often considered the world's first skyscraper, was completed in 1885|alt=A ten-story square commercial building of various Romanesque designs of its floors, seen at a 3/4 view]]
[[File:APA Australia Building in Melbourne.jpg|thumb|[[APA Building, Melbourne|APA Building]] (c. 1889–1890) in [[Melbourne, Australia]], an example of an early skyscraper outside of North America]]
There is academic disagreement over which building should be considered the first skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=5}}; {{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=114}}</ref> Identifying the first "true skyscraper" is not straightforward, and various candidates exist depending on the criteria applied.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=23}}</ref> George Post's New York [[Equitable Life Building (New York City)|Equitable Life Building]] of 1870, for example, was the first tall office building to use the elevator, while his [[2 Broadway|Produce Exchange]] building of 1884 made substantial structural advances in metal frame design.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=116–117}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=23}}</ref> The [[Home Insurance Building]] in Chicago, opened in 1885, is, however, most often labeled the first skyscraper because of its innovative use of structural steel in a metal frame design.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=5}}; {{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=115}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=22}}</ref>

The Home Insurance Building was a {{convert|138|ft|adj=on}} tall, 10-story skyscraper designed by [[William Le Baron Jenney]], who had been trained as an engineer in France and was a leading architect in Chicago.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=123–124}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=22}}</ref>{{refn|Sources during the period covered by this article often vary in their calculation of how many stories an early skyscraper had, depending on how they were counted and what material the writer drew on.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=xiv–xv}}</ref>|group=nb}} Jenney's design was unusual in that it incorporated [[structural steel]] into the building's internal metal frame alongside the traditional wrought iron. This frame took the weight of the floors of the building and helped to support the weight of the external walls as well, proving an important step towards creating the genuine non-structural [[curtain wall (architecture)|curtain walls]] that became a feature of later skyscrapers.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|pp=124–125}}</ref> The design was not perfect – some of the weight was still carried by masonry walls, and the metal frame was bolted, rather than [[rivet]]ed, together – but it was clearly a significant advance in tall building construction.<ref name="Condit 1968 125"/>

The approach quickly caught on in Chicago. In 1889 the [[Tacoma Building (Chicago)|Tacoma Building]] replaced the bolted metal design with a stronger riveted approach, and Chicago's Chamber of Commerce Building introduced interior [[lightwell|light courts]] to the structural design of skyscrapers.<ref name=ConditP126>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=126}}</ref> The 1890 [[Rand McNally Building]] became the first entirely self-supporting, steel-framed skyscraper.<ref name=ConditP126/> Some buildings, such as [[Rookery Building|The Rookery]] and the [[Monadnock Building]], combined elements of both the newer and older styles, but generally Chicago rapidly adopted steel structures as a flexible and effective way to produce a range of tall buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=127}}</ref> [[Structural engineer]]s specializing in the steel frame design began to establish practices in Chicago.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=20}}</ref>

[[File:Potter_Building.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Potter Building]], New York, built 1883&ndash;1886|alt=A lavishly-decorated red brick building seen at a 3/4 view]]

There was a boom in skyscraper construction in Chicago from 1888 onwards.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=5}}</ref> By 1893, Chicago had built 12 skyscrapers between 16 and 20 stories tall, tightly clustered in the center of the financial district.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=50}}; {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=112}}</ref> Chicago's skyscrapers, however, were constrained by the contemporary limits of steel-frame design and the muddy sub-soil in the city, which together limited most of its skyscrapers to around 16 or 17 stories.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=52}}</ref> Chicago's skyscrapers rapidly became tourist destinations for the views of the wider city they provided from their upper floors and as attractive sites in their own right.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=114–115}}</ref> Tourists were advised to hire cabs for street tours of the skyscrapers – by lying back in the cab, they would be able to safely take in the tops of the tall buildings.<ref name="Bluestone 1991 145">{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=145}}</ref>

{{Gilded Age}}The [[Masonic Temple (Chicago)|Masonic Temple]] was the most prominent of these skyscrapers. Built by the [[Freemasonry|Freemasons]] of Chicago in 1892, at a time when the Masons were a fast-growing social community, the lavish {{convert|302|ft|adj=on}} tall skyscraper had 19 stories, the bottom ten holding shops and the higher levels containing the Masons' private suites and meeting halls, some able to hold up to 1,300 people.<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|p=101}}</ref> At the top was a roof garden and observation gallery.<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|pp=108, 113}}</ref> The Freemasons were competing with their local rivals the [[Independent Order of Odd Fellows|Odd Fellows]], who intended to build a much higher skyscraper, {{convert|556|ft}} tall, that they announced would be the tallest building in the world.<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|pp=103–104, 106}}</ref> Newspapers picked up the story, circulating facts about the size of the Temple and making comparison to historical buildings such as the [[United States Capitol|Capitol]] or the [[Statue of Liberty]].<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|pp=108, 110}}</ref> The Odd Fellows project failed, but the Masonic Temple capitalized on the publicity, being declared the "tallest commercial building in the world".<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|p=114}}</ref>{{refn|Despite the positive publicity at the time, the stores in the Masonic Temple had mostly failed by 1897.<ref>{{harvnb|Wolner|2005|p=112}}</ref>|group=nb}}

In comparison, New York trailed behind Chicago, having only four buildings over 16 stories tall by 1893.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=50}}</ref> Part of the delay was caused by the slowness of the city authorities to authorize metal-frame construction techniques; it was not until 1889 that they relented and allowed [[Bradford Gilbert]] to construct the [[Tower Building (New York City)|Tower Building]], an 11-story iron-framed skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=9}}; {{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=118}}</ref> This encouraged the building of more skyscrapers in New York, although the city remained cautious about the technology for some years.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=9}}; {{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=119}}</ref> Finally, in 1895 a breakthrough was made with the construction of the [[American Surety Building]], a twenty-story, {{convert|303|ft|adj=on}} high-steel development that broke Chicago's height record.<ref name=ConditP119>{{harvnb|Condit|1968|p=119}}</ref> From then on, New York thoroughly embraced skeleton frame construction.<ref name=ConditP119/> In particular, New York newspaper companies adopted the skyscraper, building several along [[Park Row (Manhattan)|Park Row]], sometimes termed "Newspaper Row", in the 1880s and 1890s.<ref>{{harvnb|Gray|2005|pp=95–96}}</ref> A few early skyscrapers were also constructed in Baltimore, Boston, Pittsburgh, St. Louis, Rochester, and Buffalo, such as the [[Wainwright Building]], [[Wilder Building]], [[Equitable Building (Baltimore)|Equitable Building]], and [[Prudential (Guaranty) Building|Guaranty Building]].<ref>{{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=25}}; {{harvnb|Revell|2005|p=43}}; refs for buildings needed.</ref> Early examples on the [[West Coast of the United States|West Coast]] include the [[Old Chronicle Building]] and the [[Call Building]] in [[San Francisco]],<ref>{{harvnb|Tobriner|2006|pp=86–90}}</ref> as well as the [[Luzon Building]] in [[Tacoma, Washington]].<ref>{{harvnb|Gallacci|Karabaich|2009|p=42}}</ref> Early skyscrapers outside the United States include the [[APA Building, Melbourne|APA Building]] (c. 1889–1890) in [[Melbourne]], Australia, the [[Ryōunkaku]] (1890) in [[Tokyo]], Japan and the [[Witte Huis]] (1898) in [[Rotterdam]], the Netherlands.

===Architectural challenges===
{{main|Chicago school (architecture)|l1=Chicago School of Architecture|Architecture of New York City}}
[[File:Chicago Masonic Temple Building.jpg|thumb|Chicago's [[Masonic Temple (Chicago)|Masonic Temple Building]] depicted in 1909, showing the tripartite division of the building's exterior and the typical Chicago window bays|alt=A drawing of a large building, triple-bayed with wide swathes of a flat facade between the bays, topped with two hipped roofs on either end and a mansard roof in the middle]]
The architects of early skyscrapers faced a number of challenges. The most fashionable architectural style in the late 19th century was the French [[Beaux-Arts architecture|Beaux-Arts]] movement, sometimes termed the Italian Renaissance style, which applied [[Classical architecture|Classical]] aesthetic principles to modern buildings.<ref name=LandauConditP185>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=185}}</ref> American architects trained in the Beaux-Arts style at the Parisian [[Académie des Beaux-Arts]] began to return home in the 1880s, bringing these ideals and standards with them. Applying contemporary Beaux-Arts standards to early skyscrapers, however, was not straightforward. The buildings that the Beaux-Arts movement influenced were typically much shorter and broader than any skyscraper, as it was difficult to accurately reproduce the style in a tall, narrow building.<ref name=LandauConditP185/>
[[File:Monadnock Building1.JPG|left|thumb|Monadnock Building (1891–1893) was intentionally commissioned to be built with no external ornamentation]]
Skyscrapers were also primarily commercial buildings, and economics as well as aesthetics had to play an important part in their design.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=14–15}}</ref> The architectural writer Barr Ferree noted in 1893 that "current American architecture is not a matter of art, but of business. A building must pay, or there will be no investor ready with the money to meet its cost. This is at once the curse and the glory of American architecture."<ref>{{harvnb|Ferree|1893|p=231}} cited {{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=15}}</ref> George Hill echoed the theme, condemning unnecessary features on the basis that "every cubic foot that is used for purely ornamental purposes beyond that needed to express its use and to make it harmonize with others of its class, is a waste".<ref>{{harvnb|Hill|1904|p=313}} cited {{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=15}}</ref> [[Monadnock Building|Monadnock Block]], the tallest [[Load-bearing wall|load-bearing]] brick building ever constructed, is an example of such a strict approach.

By the 1890s, Chicago architects were producing a solution to this problem, creating a new architectural style, often termed the "Chicago school of architecture".<ref name="Willis 1995 11">{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=11}}</ref>{{refn|Although often being referred to as the "Chicago school of architecture" it is unclear if there was an organised body of architectural thought in Chicago during the period and the views of individual architects varied on many issues.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=105–106}}; {{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=11}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=21}}</ref>|group=nb}} The school included architects such as [[Louis Sullivan]] and [[Dankmar Adler]], Jenney, [[John Wellborn Root|John Root]], and [[William Holabird]] and [[Martin Roche]], whose designs combined architectural aesthetic theory with practical commercial sense. They favoured placing rich, ornate designs on the outside of skyscrapers at the ground level and simpler, plainer ornamentation on the upper levels, with strong vertical lines.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=143–144}}; {{harvnb|Bragdon|2003|p=158}}</ref> The roofs of their skyscrapers typically formed a comprehensible outline and structure when seen at a distance as part of the city skyline. The intent was to draw the observer's eye upwards, celebrating what Sullivan termed the "lofty" nature of the skyscraper, but not wasting resources on intricate detailing unlikely to appeal to a busy businessman.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=143–144}}; {{harvnb|Bragdon|2003|p=158}}; Root, p.71, cited {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=115}}</ref> At the same time, the more lavish ground floor designs would make the building stand out to passers-by and pull in the necessary business for a successful commercial building.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=144–145}}</ref>

[[File:New York Times Building 41 Park Row from north.jpg|thumb|left|The [[New York Times Building (41 Park Row)|New York Times Building]] in 2012, showing the multitude of different styles on a single façade typical of the city's early skyscrapers|alt=A multi-story white Romanesque building, seen looking up from street level]]
This community also saw close collaboration between architects, specialist structural engineers, and building contractors emerge on the new skyscraper projects.<ref name="Fenske 2005 21">{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=21}}</ref> Historically the industry had been dominated by individuals and small firms who combined the roles of architect and engineer, but this broke down in Chicago during the period, being replaced by a partnership between specialist architects who focused on the appearance of the skyscraper, and specialist engineers who focused on the structures that enabled it to be built.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|pp=26–27}}</ref> Chicago architectural firms grew to be large, hierarchical and with numerous specialist staff; the [[D. H. Burnham & Company]], for example, felt like a small factory to visitors, and ultimately expanded to employ 180 staff.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=24}}</ref>

The resulting [[Chicago school (architecture)|Chicago school]] produced large, solid-looking skyscrapers, built with a common appearance and to a common height.<ref name="Willis 1995 11"/> The result was usually a box-like ''palazzo'', illuminated with a large light court, ideally, if space allowed, in the center.<ref name="Willis 1995 23">{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=23}}</ref> The outside of the building was commonly divided into three parts: a base, middle section and the roof line. This tripartite design was intended both to emulate classical columns, and reflect the functions of the different parts of the skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=185–186}}</ref> The central court could form a simple courtyard, but many companies preferred to roof over the courtyard with glass to produce an [[Atrium (architecture)|atrium]] for shops and restaurants.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=57}}</ref> Rents for these shops were up to five or six times that for office space, and made an important difference to the income from a property.<ref name="Willis 1995 58">{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=58}}</ref> Chicago skyscraper windows were also a feature of the style; these were large, fixed windows flanked by smaller [[sash window]]s on either side, which provided access to sunlight and adequate ventilation. Sometimes these protruded from the building to form a slight bay.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=135}}</ref>

Although the exterior of the Chicago skyscrapers buildings were relatively plain, the entrance ways and lobbies were fitted out in a grand style.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=119}}</ref> The [[Unity Building (Chicago)|Unity Building]], for example, was reported as including "Numidian, Alps, Green and Sienna marbles&nbsp;... an artistic screen of glass and bronze&nbsp;... a marble balcony" alongside "Corinthian columns with finely carved capitals, gold-leaf and silver chandeliers, and silver-plated latticework" on the elevators.<ref>{{harvnb|Flinn|1893|p=197}} cited {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=119}}; {{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=119}}</ref> The aim was to project a sense of prosperity and solid financial credentials, which in turn would attract tenants willing to pay high rents.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=123}}</ref> For the tenants, such surroundings were good for their own business credibility and affirmed their own social status as professionals.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=123–138}}</ref>

New York faced similar architectural challenges, but in comparison to Chicago, skyscraper architects worked less closely with engineers and other specialists, and instead held strong backgrounds in the Beaux Arts movement and perceived their role to be primarily artistic rather than a partnership with the mechanical arts.<ref name="Fenske 2005 21"/> Their practices tended to be smaller, resembling ''atelier'' style workshops.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=25}}</ref> Structural engineers in New York took longer to build up a strong professional role there, a trend reflected in the lower engineering quality of many early skyscrapers in the city.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=27}}</ref> The New York style emphasized stunning height and a somewhat eclectic use of architectural features from other periods, creating an energetic, flamboyant appearance.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=11–12}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=26}}</ref> Towers were common, making best use of the relatively small plots of land in New York.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=23, 40}}</ref> Some New York skyscrapers emulated the tripartite style of Chicago, but others broke their exterior down into many different layers, each with its own style.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=186}}</ref> Proponents argued that this reintroduced a sense of human proportion to these tall buildings; critics felt that the results were confusing and ungainly.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=184–186}}</ref>

===Life in early skyscrapers===
[[File:Plan of Chicago Stock Exchange.png|thumb|Plan of a typical level of the [[Chicago Stock Exchange|Chicago Stock Exchange Building]], 1893:
{{image key|
|list type=bulleted
|A: Court
|B: Hall
|C: Toilet
|D: Barbershop
|E: Vents
|F: [[Flue]]
|G: Office, {{convert|12|ft}} by {{convert|19|ft}}
}}
|alt=A cross-sectional look at a single story of a building; refer to caption for more information]]
Early skyscrapers were mainly made up of small office cubicles, commonly only {{convert|12|ft}} across, which were placed adjacent to one another along long corridors, following a pattern first invented in the [[Oriel Chambers]] building in England in 1864.<ref name=FordP24>{{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=24}}</ref> This allowed the average small company to rent a small amount of space using one or two offices, but held out the option for future expansion by renting additional office cubicles if required at a later date.<ref name=FordP24/> A skyscraper office relied on natural sunlight from the windows but if necessary was dimly lit from electric desk-top lamps.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=24}}</ref> By the standards of the day, these offices were very modern, with radiators, air vents, and the latest fixtures and fittings, and modern communication systems, including telephone and [[pneumatic tube]]s were often installed.<ref name=BluestonePP128>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=128, 132}}</ref> As a result, many businesses chose to move out of their older, low-rise offices in Chicago to take up tenancy in the new skyscrapers, which were felt to be more convenient and healthier.<ref name=BluestonePP128/>

The first skyscrapers were mainly occupied by male workers, but this changed during the 1890s, with female employees becoming more common. The percentage of female clerical workers in Chicago, for example, increased from 11 percent in 1880 to 21 percent by 1890, reaching 30 percent by 1900.<ref>{{harvnb|Fine|2005|pp=64–65, 69}}</ref> Various moral concerns were raised about men and women mixing in such offices, which were characterized as being masculine spaces, full of tobacco smoke and profanity and therefore unsuitable for women.<ref>{{harvnb|Fine|2005|pp=68–70}}</ref> The new female workers typically worked as typists or [[stenographer]]s, using the recently invented [[typewriter]], which grew in number in U.S. offices from 146 in 1879 to 65,000 by 1890.<ref>{{harvnb|Fine|2005|p=73}}</ref>

Skyscrapers provided a wide range of in-house services for their tenants, including shops, restaurants, barbers, tobacconists, newsagents, tailors, professional specialists and libraries.<ref name=BluestoneP141>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=141}}</ref> Skyscrapers also employed a substantial number of service staff to maintain and support them; a building such as the Chicago Board of Trade spent 20 percent of its rental revenue on service staff, employing 41 people, including janitors, elevator operators, engineers, and an electrician.<ref name=BluestoneP141/> With this collection of services and facilities, skyscrapers of the period were often referred to as small cities in their own right.<ref name="Bluestone 1991 145"/>

===Criticism and reform in Chicago===

Opposition to Chicago's skyscrapers began to grow during the late 1880s and early 1890s.<ref name=BluestoneP150>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=150}}</ref> Even before the development of the skyscraper, some criticized large buildings in Chicago for dominating churches and private houses, and this sentiment strengthened.<ref>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|pp=5, 150}}</ref> Critics complained that the concentration of tall buildings in the center of the city was causing huge congestion, and each new skyscraper was also burning additional coal to power its facilities, together consuming a total of over one million tons each year, leaving smoke and stagnant air hanging over Chicago.<ref name=BluestoneP150/> Many were concerned over the risk of a major fire breaking out and spreading, uncontrolled, from building to building.<ref name=BluestoneP150/>

Chicago was not alone in having concerns over the growth of the skyscraper. In Boston, the [[Fiske Building|Fiske]] and the [[Ames Building]]s were built in the late 1880s, {{convert|183|ft|abbr=on}} and {{convert|190|ft}} tall respectively, but protests by local civic campaigners and the real estate industry resulted in the city passing a law to limit new buildings to a maximum of {{convert|123|ft}}, effectively banning the construction of skyscrapers.<ref name=RevellP43>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|p=43}}</ref> The cities of Philadelphia, Los Angeles and Washington D.C. similarly introduced height restriction laws to limit skyscraper construction.<ref>{{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=31}}</ref>

The decisive factor in favor of change in Chicago, however, was the economic slowdown in the early 1890s, which gave way to the financial [[panic of 1893]].<ref name=BluestonsP150WillisP9>{{harvnb|Bluestone|1991|p=150}}; {{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=9}}</ref> The recession, combined with the frantic building of the previous few years, meant that Chicago suddenly had a significant surplus of office space, threatening occupancy levels and rents.<ref name=BluestonsP150WillisP9/> Regulation was introduced by the city council to control the problem in 1892, with support from the real estate industry who hoped to slow the construction of additional office space and shore up their diminishing profit margins.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=9}}</ref> The height of new buildings was limited to {{convert|150|ft}}, with lower height levels on narrower streets, effectively curtailing the construction of any taller skyscrapers.<ref name=BluestonsP150WillisP9/>

==The "First Great Age": 1900–1919==
[[File:The Skyscrapers of New York (1906).webm|thumb|''The Skyscrapers of New York'', a 1906 film|alt=An 11-minute silent documentary on tall buildings in New York City]]

===Pre-war boom===

The early years of the 20th century saw a range of technically sophisticated, architecturally confident skyscrapers built in New York; academics [[Sarah Landau]] and [[Carl Condit]] term this "the first great age" of skyscraper building.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=298, 395}}</ref> Some were relatively conservative buildings in a classical style, such as the Mutual Life, [[Atlantic Mutual Insurance Company|Atlantic Mutual]], and [[Broad Exchange Building]]s, all designed by [[Clinton and Russell]].<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=288–399}}</ref> Others broke new ground, including the [[Flatiron Building]] which opened in 1903 near Madison Square.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=301}}</ref> The Chicago firm of Daniel Hudson Burnham designed the {{convert|307|ft}} high, 21 story structure; the unusually shaped, narrow building needed particularly strong wind bracing, while the facade was richly textured and incorporated stylistic features more common in Chicago.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=302–304}}</ref> A critical and popular success, the Flatiron was likened to the [[Parthenon]] of Ancient Greece and became a New York icon.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=302–304}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=38}}</ref>

The construction of the [[Singer Tower]] was announced by the company in 1906, who intended to produce the tallest skyscraper in the world.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=354–355}}</ref> The company already had several low-rise buildings in New York that the tower would be incorporated into and planned to rent out the bottom half of the tower to tenants to subsidize their use of the upper half.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=355}}</ref> The skyscraper was designed by [[Ernest Flagg]], a Beaux-Arts advocate and noted critic of existing skyscrapers, who justified taking on the project as a way of generating support for skyscraper reform.<ref name="Fenske 2005 22">{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=22}}</ref> The design was technically challenging: the tall, narrow tower needed special wind bracing, and the deep bedrock on the site required particularly deep foundations.<ref name="Landau 1996 357">{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=357}}</ref> The tower was faced in dark brick and followed the Beaux-Arts style used by the rest of the complex, with a galleried lobby fitted out in Italian marble.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=359–361}}</ref> When it opened in 1908, it had 41 stories and was {{convert|612|ft}} tall; visitors paid $0.50 ($14 in 2020 terms) each to use the observation area at the top of the building.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=354}}</ref>

[[File:Woolworth Building and City Hall Park, New York City 1910s retouched.png|thumb|left|Color postcard of "The [[Woolworth Building]] and [[New York City Hall|City Hall Park]], New York City", around 1913, when the Woolworth was the world's tallest building|alt=Refer to caption]]

The [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower]] was opened in 1909, the culmination of a long building project by [[Napoleon LeBrun|N. LeBrun and Sons]] to hold Metropolitan Life's growing headquarters staff, 2,800 strong by 1909.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|pp=120–125}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=361}}</ref> At {{convert|700|ft}} high and with 50 stories, it became the world's new tallest building.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|pp=123–125}}</ref> Metropolitan Life intended the skyscraper to promote the company's image, and the building was surrounded by publicity.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|pp=125–126}}</ref> The tower was featured on the front of prominent magazines such as ''[[Scientific American]]'', as well as on the sides of [[corn flake]] boxes, coffee packets, and cars.<ref name=MoudryPP126>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|pp=126–127}}</ref>{{refn|Metropolitan Life valued the free publicity surrounding its skyscraper building at over $440,000 ($198 million in 2010 terms).<ref name=MoudryPP126/>|group=nb}} The tower was loosely modeled on the Venetian [[St Mark's Campanile]], and featured extensive Early Renaissance-style detailing, with the more modern additions of huge clock faces, electric floodlights for night-time illumination, and an observation deck at the top.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|p=125}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=361, 364–366}}</ref> The design won critical acclaim within the American architectural profession.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=366–367}}</ref>

The construction of the [[Woolworth Building]] was announced in 1910 by [[Frank Winfield Woolworth|Frank Woolworth]], who wanted to create the largest income-producing property in the U.S.<ref name=LandauConditPP381>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=381–382}}</ref> The project grew, and Woolworth finally opted for a 55-story, {{convert|792|ft|adj=on}} high skyscraper, the latest tallest building in the world, at a cost of $13.5 million ($5.1 billion in 2010 terms).<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=381–382}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=42}}</ref>{{refn|Prices in this article are given in US dollars throughout. Equivalent modern prices have been given in 2010 US dollars to two significant figures. The equivalent prices of modern goods and services – such as entry costs to skyscrapers – have been calculated using the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The CPI is not reliable for comparing the value of capital investment projects – such as the cost or value of early skyscrapers – over time, and these have been calculated using the relative share of GDP index.<ref>{{cite web| title = Seven Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a US Dollar Amount&nbsp;– 1774 to Present| publisher = MeasuringWorth| year = 2012| url = http://www.measuringworth.com/uscompare/ | access-date = September 8, 2012}}</ref>|group=nb}} Architect [[Cass Gilbert]] designs included a very high proportion of usable – and thus rentable – floor space, with a great deal of light and a flexible floor plan that could be subdivided for different tenants.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=383–384}}</ref> Up-to-date fittings were installed to encourage a high-class of tenants, including the world's fastest elevators, safety features, and a swimming pool.<ref name="Landau 1996 386">{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=386}}</ref> Gilbert adopted the Beaux-Arts style, using accented terracotta and glass to emphasis vertical lines, elegantly echoing the structural frame underneath and incorporating 15th and 16th century [[Flamboyant Gothic]]-styled features. It was capped by a gilded tower that blended into the sky behind it to produce an illusion of even greater height.<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|pp=20. 29}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=384, 387}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=44}}</ref> The building was illuminated with floodlights at night, topped with red and white flashing lights.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=390}}</ref> It was famously dubbed the "Cathedral of Commerce", rather to Gilbert's displeasure as he had attempted to avoid copying ecclesiastical architecture.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=382, 387}}</ref>

Meanwhile, Chicago's skyscraper industry also boomed during the decade before [[World War I]]. The city's [[Chicago "L"|elevated train network]] was operating by 1910, allowing more workers to come into downtown.<ref name=FineP66>{{harvnb|Fine|2005|p=66}}</ref> In 1910 alone {{convert|1500000|sqft|m2|sigfig=2}} of new offices were opened and by the end of the decade, Chicago had the second largest number of headquarters offices in the U.S.<ref name=FineP66/> Chicago architectural firms such as Daniel H. Burnham and then [[Graham, Anderson, Probst & White]] continued to design skyscrapers in the ''palazzo'' style made popular in the previous decade.<ref name="Willis 1995 58"/> Chicago had hosted the [[World's Columbian Exposition]] in 1893, a massive international event which had excited interest in the themes of classical architecture and well-designed city landscapes.<ref name="Willis 1995 59">{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=59}}</ref> Chicago also had extensive discussions in 1909 about the potential for designing large parts of the city, the [[Burnham Plan of Chicago]].<ref name="Willis 1995 59"/>

The resulting skyscrapers reflected these debates: the [[Santa Fe Building (Chicago)|Railway Exchange]], the [[Peoples Gas Building|Peoples Gas]] and the [[Continental Illinois|Illinois Continental and Commercial Bank Buildings]] were each substantial, quarter-block wide ''palazzo'' cubes of common height, their facades divided into a classical tripartite design, and sporting classical columns and other features.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=58–60}}</ref> Despite the apparent uniformity of design, individual buildings varied considerably in the detail of their designs in effort to express their particular identities, the Peoples Gas Building using texture and the Railway Exchange Building's white terracotta, for example.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruegmann|1997|p=141}}</ref>

===Improvements in construction===
[[File:Typical floor of the Flatiron Building.jpg|thumb|Typical floor of the [[Flatiron Building]]|alt=A cross-sectional drawing of a typical story in the Flatiron Building]]
The process of building skyscrapers became more sophisticated, starting with the acquisition of the real estate needed for the site.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=160–162}}</ref> Brokers working on commission would secretly acquire the individual lots of land required for a project, operating under a variety of names to avoid having the price increase once a planned build became known.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=160–161}}</ref> The properties at the front of the site would typically be bought first, so if news broke of the skyscraper then those owning property at the back of the plot would have little choice but to sell anyway.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=161}}</ref> The funding for skyscraper developments was normally lent by banks, insurance companies, or raised through [[Corporate bond|bonds]] sold through a specialised bond house, with the latter becoming increasingly popular after World War I.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=162}}</ref>

Efforts were made to improve the processes for erecting skyscrapers, largely through the work of general contractors such as Louis Horowitz and [[Frank Bunker Gilbreth, Sr.|Frank Gilbreth]], who in turn drew on recent work by efficiency specialist [[Frederick Winslow Taylor|Frederick Taylor]].<ref>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|pp=32–33}}</ref> Time schedules were devised for all the work to be undertaken, with costs carefully monitored and reports produced each day.<ref name=FenskeP33>{{harvnb|Fenske|2005|p=33}}</ref> The results were demonstrated on the Woolworth Building construction project, where {{convert|1153|t|kg}} of steel were assembled in only six days, a record for the period.<ref name=FenskeP33/> Improved windbracing techniques were introduced.<ref name="Landau 1996 357"/> The use of pneumatic caissons in skyscraper foundations grew more advanced; in the construction of the 1908 [[Manhattan Municipal Building]] they were successfully sunk {{convert|144|ft}} below the surface, with specially conditioned workers operating in shifts with constant medical support.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=373–374}}</ref>

New technologies were also introduced within the buildings. Fast [[Otis Elevator Company|Otis]] elevators, powered by electricity rather than steam-driven hydraulics, began to be installed in skyscrapers, with Ellithorpe safety air cushions protecting the passengers in the case of failure.<ref name="Landau 1996 386"/> Lighting improved, with the recommended levels in 1916 being around twice the level of the 1890s.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=24–25}}</ref> Nonetheless, skyscrapers still relied primarily on natural sunlight, which required installing large windows and having tall ceilings to allow the sunlight to penetrate the back of the offices; an office deeper than {{convert|28|ft}} was not considered a practical design.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=25–26}}</ref>

===Life in the skyscrapers===
[[File:Met Life Acturial Office, 1910.jpg|thumb|left|Working conditions in the [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower]], 1910|alt=A drawing of workers at desks and in cubicles]]

One of the reasons for the increase in the numbers of skyscrapers during this period was the growth in demand for office workers. In part this demand was fuelled by many U.S. firms becoming larger and more complex, and white-collar sectors such as insurance and banking grew in scale.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldin|Katz|2008|p=172}}</ref> It was also driven by changing technology. The typewriter was joined in the office by the [[adding machine]], the telephone and filing cabinets, all adding to the demand for office space and requiring increasingly specialised workers.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldin|Katz|2008|pp=172–173}}</ref>

Tenants and rental income were essential to the financial success of any skyscraper, as even the largest skyscrapers and those founded by prominent companies rented out much of their office space.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=147–148}}</ref> Owners could charge significantly more for office space close to the main windows, making it most efficient to build skyscrapers with as much premium office space as possible, even if this cost slightly more to construct in the first instance.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=26–27}}</ref> As a result, a standard pattern for office units in both New York and Chicago emerged, with either a single rectangular office adjoining an exterior wall, or a T-shaped design, with a reception room giving way to two windowed offices, separated by glass partitions.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=27–28}}</ref> Skyscrapers usually took on large numbers of relatively small companies as their tenants. A skyscraper such as the Woolworth Building had around 600 different tenants in 1913, for example; a typical tenant might rent four or five office units in a skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=28–29, 148}}</ref>

=== Criticism ===
[[File:Stieglitz-NewYorkOldNew.jpg|thumb|[[Alfred Stieglitz]]'s 1910 work ''Old and New New York'', showing the [[4 Park Avenue|Vanderbilt Hotel]] under construction|alt=A sepia view of 19th-century Italianate mansions being dwarfed by a steel-girder structure, the core of the future Vanderbilt Hotel]]

Skyscrapers, particularly those in New York, attracted considerable comment, much of it negative. On his return to New York, writer [[Henry James]] condemned the buildings in ''The American Scene'' as simply "giants of the mere market", "mercenary monsters" doomed to be torn down in turn as other, even larger, buildings took their place.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=8}}; {{harvnb|Bragdon|2003|p=155}}</ref> In Chicago the combination of the environmental pollution and skyscrapers meant that, as Charles Warner complained, "one can scarcely see across the streets on a damp day, and the huge buildings loom up in the black sky in ghostly dimness".<ref>{{harvnb|Cronon|1992|p=12}}</ref>

Wider artistic sentiments varied. Many, like [[Alfred Stieglitz]], harboured mixed feelings over New York's skyscrapers, reflected in his famous 1903 portrait of the [[Flatiron Building]], and his 1910 work ''Old and New New York'' that contrasts the growing steel frame of the emerging [[Vanderbilt Hotel]] with the old low-rise blocks of the street below.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|pp=42–44}}</ref> Poets also wrote about the issues, the [[Modernist poetry|early Modernist]] [[Sadakichi Hartmann]] describing how "from the city's stir and madd'ning roar" the Flatiron's "monstrous shape soars in massive flight".<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=46}}</ref> Artists such as [[Alvin Langdon Coburn|Alvin Coburn]] and [[John Marin]] experimented with producing portraits of New York's skyscrapers, capturing the positive and negative aspects of the modern structures.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|pp=46–55}}</ref> In 1908 artist Harry Pettit produced a romantic interpretation of a future New York, filled with giant skyscrapers supporting aerial bridges and receiving dirigibles from around the globe.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|pp=9–10}}</ref>

Amongst the architectural community, the Exposition in Chicago inspired many Americans to champion planning cities that had a unified design, in which each building had unique features but elegantly complemented its neighbours, typically by being built to a common height: "horizontal visual unity".<ref>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=38–39}}</ref> In the aftermath of the Exposition, many of these advocates joined with the Beaux-Arts movement to form the [[City Beautiful movement]], proposing low-rise cities with wide boulevards, built in a classical style.<ref>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|p=30}}</ref> These critics condemned New York's skyscrapers, [[Montgomery Schuyler]] describing how they had produced a "horribly jagged sierra" of a city skyline and complaining that no modern skyscraper had turned out to be an architectural success.<ref>{{harvnb|Schuyler|1961|p=443}} cited {{harvnb|Revell|2005|p=39}}; {{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=39–40}}</ref> [[Charles Rollinson Lamb|Charles Lamb]] argued that the skyscraper impinged on the rights of the rest of the city by destroying the collective appearance of an urban area.<ref>{{harvnb|Lamb|1898|p=57}} cited {{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=41–42}}</ref> Some architects, such as [[Charles Follen McKim|Charles McKim]] and [[Stanford White]] refused to work on such projects altogether.<ref name="Fenske 2005 22"/>

===Reform in New York===

Calls were made in New York for legislation to prevent the growth of skyscrapers, citing their effect on the city skylines, but these attempts faced legal obstacles. The [[United States Constitution]] did not give local government authority to prevent the buildings on the grounds of aesthetics alone, and any such law in New York was considered likely to face judicial challenge.<ref>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=42–43}}</ref>

Others argued that legal reform of skyscraper construction was needed for public health and safety reasons, an area in which U.S. law was normally more supportive of state intervention.<ref name=RevellP43/> The risk of fire was one concern; while skyscrapers might be relatively fireproof, their height made conventional fire-fighting difficult. Architect Charles Bragdon considered a large scale, devastating high-rise fire to be inevitable if regulation was not forthcoming.<ref>{{harvnb|Bragdon|2003|pp=155–156}}</ref> The [[Great Baltimore Fire|Baltimore fire of 1904]] was widely cited as an example of this risk and, although Baltimore had few high rise buildings, city lawyers argued that the taller buildings had caused the flames to spread through the city during the blaze.<ref name=RevellP43/> Baltimore subsequently passed a law in 1904, banning buildings higher than {{convert|70|ft}}.<ref name=RevellP43/> Other campaigners argued that skyscrapers were compromising access to light and air, noting that when tall buildings rose straight up from the sidewalk, they cast long shadows across the street, preventing healthy sunlight from reaching smaller buildings below.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|pp=393–395}}</ref>

[[File:Equitable Building.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Equitable Building (Manhattan)|Equitable Building]] in 2011, showing the effect of pre-zoning skyscrapers when seen from the sidewalk|alt=A street-level picture looking up at an imposing building, demonstrating its shadowing effects]]
Early attempts by Ernest Flagg to limit the height of New York's skyscrapers in 1896 failed; further unsuccessful attempts followed between 1906 and 1908, and legislation was turned down again in 1909, partially because of pressure from the real estate industry.<ref name=WillisP68>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=68}}</ref> After 1913, however, the property market in New York entered a recession, and vacancy levels in buildings began to rise.<ref name=WillisP68/> The campaign for change was helped by the construction of the [[Equitable Building (Manhattan)|Equitable Building]] in 1915 at the estimated cost of $29 million ($10.9 billion in 2010 terms), which rapidly became infamous as its vast height and bulk blocked views cast neighbours into permanent shade.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=69}}; {{harvnb|American Art Publishing|1918|p=11}}</ref> The real estate industry finally ceased its objections to new legislation, and the [[1916 Zoning Resolution]] was passed.<ref name=WillisP68/>

The details of the legislation were largely the work of architect George Ford. Ford had sympathies with the City Beautiful movement, disliked the unimaginative form of many New York skyscrapers, and had concerns over urban public health, but he also found tall buildings exciting and believed that horizontal visual unity produced boring architecture.<ref>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=47–48}}</ref> As a consequence of Ford's influence, New York's laws were relatively complex and divided up the city into different zones; in each zone, a particular [[Zoning in the United States|zoning envelope]] applied, controlling the height to which buildings could be built.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=67}}; {{harvnb|Revell|2005|pp=48–49}}</ref> Typically a building could only rise up from the sidewalk vertically by around {{convert|100|ft}}, after which the building had to be [[setback (architecture)|set back]] at a set angle to allow sunlight to reach the street below.<ref name=WillisP67>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=67}}</ref> On a quarter of the site, however, the owner could build as high as they wished, without any further restrictions.<ref name=WillisP67/>

==Interwar period, boom and depression: 1920–1939==

===Post-war boom===
[[File:J34 636 Palacio Salvo.jpg|alt=|thumb|The [[Palacio Salvo]] of [[Montevideo]] built in 1928 at its completion it was the tallest reinforced concrete structure.]]
A real estate boom occurred in the U.S. after the end of the war, with a particular surge in the construction of new skyscrapers between 1925 and 1931.<ref name="Schleier 1986 69">{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=69}}</ref> In New York, a quarter of the financial district was rebuilt between 1928 and 1931, with {{convert|17000000|sqft|m2|sigfig=2}} of new office space added between 1925 and 1929 alone.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=165}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=xi}}</ref> In Chicago, limited wartime construction created supply shortages, and rent levels rose in response by around 100 percent between 1919 and 1924.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=109}}</ref> This level of potential profits encouraged an explosion of new building projects in the city.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=109–110}}</ref> The boom inflated prices in the real estate market, leading to speculative financing and building projects, including the introduction of 100 percent mortgages for new builds. An early edition of the ''[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]'' magazine commented wryly that "all a man needs to own a skyscraper is the money and the land. And he may be able to get along without the money."<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=109–110, 165}}</ref>

Skyscrapers continued to grow in height throughout the 1920s.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=41, 85}}</ref> In part this was the result of improvements in technology: steel-frame structures had become increasingly efficient, while improvements in elevator design made taller buildings easier to ascend.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=41–42}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=84}}</ref> Commercial factors were at work too, as growing commercial demand pushed up rents, enabling taller projects, while the higher offices attracted more sunlight, permitting the charging of premium rents.<ref name=WillisPP42>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=42–43}}</ref> The tallest buildings could also acquire publicity for their owners, in turn making it easier to find and keep the best tenants.<ref name=WillisPP42/> Furthermore, the higher the cost of the underlying real estate, the taller a building needed to be to generate a suitable return on the investment, and the minimum sensible commercial height for a skyscraper project grew to between 40 and 45 stories.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=85}}; {{harvnb|Clark|Kingston|1930}}, cited {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=55}}</ref> 70 story skyscrapers became relatively common, although an influential 1930 study demonstrated that the best rate of return on a skyscraper was to build it 63 stories high, returning an annual profit of 10.25 percent.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=86–88}}</ref>

[[File:Terminal Tower ceiling.jpg|thumb|left|Main entrance to Cleveland's [[Terminal Tower]] in 2012|alt=A golden roof of a lobby]]
Skyscrapers continued to spread both across the U.S. and internationally.
