New York and Chicago remained the center of skyscraper development, but most major cities in the U.S. had built skyscrapers by 1929, frequently as a result of competition between rival cities for status and investment.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=69}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=53}}; {{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=9}}</ref> [[Cincinnati]] built the Cincinnati Towers in 1914, followed by the [[Carew Tower|Carew Tower Complex]] in 1930.<ref name="Ford 2005 36–37, 39">{{harvnb|Ford|2005|pp=36–37, 39}}</ref> In [[Detroit]], the [[Cadillac Place|General Motors Building]] opened in 1920 and the [[Fisher Building]] in 1928.<ref name="Douglas 1996 85">{{harvnb|Douglas|1996|p=85}}</ref> [[Cleveland]] acquired the [[Huntington Bank Building|Union Trust Building]] in 1923 and the [[Terminal Tower]] in 1929; the latter, built by the [[Van Sweringen brothers]], was, for a short period, the second tallest building in the world, the tallest in the world outside of New York until 1953 and tallest in the U.S. until 1964.<ref>{{harvnb|Douglas|1996|p=85}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=38}}</ref> [[Seattle]] had built [[Smith Tower]] in 1914, and the Los Angeles local government granted itself an exemption from city planning restrictions in order to build the [[Los Angeles City Hall]] in 1928.<ref name="Ford 2005 36–37, 39"/> Also in 1928, the [[Industrial Trust Tower]] was built in [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Industrial Trust Company, Providence|url=http://www.ricurrency.com/bank-name/industrial-trust-company-providence/|publisher=RI Currency|access-date=11 April 2014}}</ref>

Skyscrapers were also built in other developed countries, although reaching nowhere near the level of construction seen in the U.S.<ref name=GoldbergerP51>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=51}}</ref> This was partially the result of a lack of funding but also because of local architectural preferences.<ref name=GoldbergerP51/> Some European cities including London and Paris had laws to ban tall buildings, but elsewhere skyscrapers began to appear, including [[Toronto]]'s [[Commerce Court|Imperial Bank of Commerce Building]], [[Antwerp]]'s [[Boerentoren]], [[Liverpool]]'s [[Royal Liver Building]], [[Madrid]]'s [[Telefónica Building]] and [[Buenos Aires]]' [[Kavanagh Building]].<ref>{{harvnb|Clark|1991|p=157}}; {{harvnb|Binder|2006|p=64}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=25}}; {{harvnb|Walter|1993|p=205}}</ref> Many other European skyscrapers were proposed in a frenzy of excited planning, although few materialised. See:[[List of early skyscrapers]]. Soviet Russia began the construction of the {{convert|1365|ft|adj=on}} [[Palace of the Soviets]] in the late 1930s, in the [[Stalinist architecture|Socialist Classicism]] style, which would have become the tallest building in the world, but war intervened and the skyscraper was never completed.<ref>{{harvnb|Binder|2006|p=10}}</ref> In the post-war years, this style resulted in the monumental [[Seven Sisters (Moscow)|Seven Sisters of Moscow]].<ref>{{harvnb|Paperny|2002}}</ref>

The technology used in constructing skyscrapers continued to develop. Time was increasingly a factor in the projects, and architects and their specialist teams developed faster ways to design and construct the buildings to minimise the interest payments during construction and hasten the arrival of rental income.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=44–45, 79}}</ref> By 1930, skyscrapers were being erected in just 12 months by teams of workers totalling 5,000 men, with four floors being assembled in a typical week.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=74}}</ref> Building skyscraper towers involved some adaption of engineering techniques, as effectively two different buildings were being designed – the base and the tower – which needed to be efficiently linked using elevators and other service facilities.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=83–85}}</ref> Most new offices settled around a standard size, {{convert|9|ft}} wide by {{convert|20|to|30|ft|abbr=on}} deep, depending on the height of the ceiling, with multiple small windows considered better than a few larger ones.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=81}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=69}}</ref> The output of electric lighting continued to improve, although this began to give off excessive heat within the offices.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=25}}</ref> Air conditioning was first installed in a few skyscrapers during the 1930s.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=26}}.</ref>

===Art Deco skyscrapers and New York's set-back style===
[[File:40 Wall Street IMG 9048.JPG|thumb|[[40 Wall Street]] in 2010, showing the setback style|alt=A street-level view looking up at a setback tower, demonstrating the sunlight allowed to the ground in contrast to the Equitable Life Building shown earlier]]
During the 1920s and 1930s many skyscrapers were designed in an [[Art Deco]] style.<ref>{{harvnb|Watkin|2005|p=580}}</ref>{{refn|The definition of architectural styles is usually imprecise. "Art Deco" was often termed "moderne" during the 1920s, and historians such as Daniel Abramson draw further contrast between styles during the period that stressed traditional, often [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic]] features; classic Art Deco styles; and more minimalist versions towards the end of the period.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=96–119}}</ref>|group=nb}} This architectural approach typically combined what Carol Willis terms an "aesthetic of simple, sculptural mass" with the use of rich colour and ornamentation on the surfaces of the buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=114}}; {{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=77–79}}</ref> The aim was to call attention to the increasingly complex three-dimensional shape of the skyscraper, in contrast to earlier styles which could be critiqued, as historian Larry Ford suggests, as being merely "short buildings made taller with additional stories".<ref>{{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=37}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=19}}</ref> Windows were de-emphasised in favour of creating a strong sense of shape and mass, the surrounding walls treated as textured fabric, dressing the building underneath.<ref>{{harvnb|Shepherd|2003|p=259}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=49}}</ref> Skyscrapers of this period typically lost their ornamental horizontal divisions, being broken up by physical changes in their shape as one looked up the building, the whole forming a striking silhouette.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=102}}; {{harvnb|Shepherd|2003|p=259}}</ref>

In New York, the 1916 act to allow light and air to reach the streets encouraged a stepped or [[ziggurat]] approach to skyscraper design; this "set-back" style often made unrestricted use of the 25 percent of the site allowed by law to complete with a very tall tower.<ref name="WillisP67"/> This encouraged a diversity of buildings, while maintaining an element of harmony and consistency of style.<ref>{{harvnb|Revell|2005|p=51}}</ref> The [[Paramount Building]] and [[120 Wall Street]], for example, were constructed in the set-back style without towers, partially because the limited size of the sites would have made the towers relatively narrow and – when packed with the necessary elevators and service facilities – economically unviable.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=72–73, 76}}</ref> Many other skyscrapers built on larger or more expensive plots opted for the tallest towers possible, including the $24 million ($3.8 billion in 2010 terms) Bank of Manhattan Building at [[40 Wall Street]] and the City Bank-Farmers Trust Company Building at [[20 Exchange Place]].<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=72–73}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=29}}</ref> New York continued its lead in tall skyscrapers throughout the period; in 1920 it had ten times the number of tall buildings than its nearest rival Chicago.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=9–10}}</ref>

Some New York skyscrapers complemented traditional, cubicle offices linked by corridors, with larger, more open-plan spaces called "general offices".<ref name=AbramsonP2001>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=122}}</ref> These maximised the number of workers that could be fitted into a given space and provided for greater flexibility.<ref name=AbramsonP2001/> Expensive corporate suites were also created during the 1930s, especially on [[Wall Street]], typically on the highest levels of the buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=123}}</ref> These were used by the corporate executives and were usually lavishly outfitted in a range of traditional and exotic styles.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=123–125}}</ref> The lobbies of these skyscrapers remained grand affairs, although some banks now eschewed renting out space to shops and restaurants in favour of a more exclusive atmosphere.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=140–145}}</ref> The largest skyscrapers held up to 16,000 workers, although between 5,000 and 10,000 was more common, and the buildings held a wide range of services to support them, including beauty salons, private luncheon clubs, chiropodists and gymnasiums.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=155–156}}</ref> A skyscraper such as the Cities Service Building at [[70 Pine Street]] directly employed over 200 staff to manage and protect the property.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=157–158}}</ref> The technology within the offices also grew still more sophisticated, with [[Dictation machine|dictating]], automatic typing and [[tabulating machine]]s being used by teams of ever more specialised office workers.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldin|Katz|2008|pp=173–14}}</ref>{{refn|In 1895, there were 15 well-defined roles in U.S. offices, with generalised labels such as clerks, office boys and bookkeepers; by 1922 increased specialisation meant that this had risen to 22, and by 1940 over a hundred distinct roles existed, including accountants, auditors, payroll clerks, stenographers, receptionists, machine operators and file clerks.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldin|Katz|2008|p=174}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|pp=160–161}}</ref>|group=nb}}

===Chicago's towers===
[[File:Chicago 29 Oct116.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Tribune Tower]] was one of the most famous buildings of the 1920s|alt=A gothic tower with a "crown" of ornament at its top]]
Chicago altered its laws in the 1920s to allow towers to be built as part of its skyscrapers. In 1920, the maximum building height in Chicago was increased to {{convert|260|ft}}, and unoccupied structures on a building, such as ornamental towers, were allowed to extend up to {{convert|400|ft}} high.<ref name=WillisP111>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=111}}</ref> Additional changes came in 1923, with taller occupied towers being permitted for the first time, but subject to controls on overall volumes.<ref name="Willis 1995 23"/> The main building of a skyscraper could be up to {{convert|264|ft}} tall, and a tower could be built on up to 25 percent of the lot, but the tower could not have a volume of more than a sixth of the main block.<ref name=WillisP111/> In practice, this meant that a tower could not be built more than around 20 stories tall in a typical Chicago skyscraper development.<ref name=WillisP111/>

Initially, Chicago still preferred ''palazzo''-styled buildings with large light courts in the centre, because they remained the most profitable designs.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=49, 111}}</ref> The [[Wrigley Building]], built under the 1920 law, demonstrated the effect of two ornamental towers on top of a skyscraper.<ref name=WillisP111/> Under the revised law, the [[Metropolitan Tower (Chicago)|Straus Building]] and the [[Pittsfield Building]] took the ''palazzo'' design and added somewhat stunted towers on top in the early 1920s, producing profitable buildings.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=112–113, 117}}</ref>

One of the period's most famous buildings, the [[Tribune Tower]], emerged from a [[architectural design competition|competition]] held by the [[Tribune Company]] in 1922 to celebrate its 75th anniversary.<ref name="Solomonson 2005 147">{{harvnb|Solomonson|2005|p=147}}</ref> The newspaper was one of the largest in the world and used the competition, in which members of the public were invited to influence the design of the skyscraper, to build a loyal following amongst its readership and generate free publicity.<ref>{{harvnb|Solomonson|2005|pp=148–150}}</ref> The final design was determined by a competition panel largely made up of the company's appointees, who chose [[John Mead Howells|John Howells]] and [[Raymond Hood]]'s tower design.<ref>{{harvnb|Solomonson|2005|p=156}}</ref> The resulting tower was a conservative, Gothic design and controversy about the decision broke out almost immediately: Louis Sullivan and many others criticized Howells and Hood's design as being derivative of the Woolworth Tower.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=112}}; {{harvnb|Solomonson|2005|p=158}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=51}}</ref> Regardless of its critics, the Tribune received as many as 20,000 visitors to its observation gallery when it opened in 1925.<ref name="Solomonson 2005 147"/> The unbuilt [[Eliel Saarinen's Tribune Tower design|second-place entry in the competition]], a more simplified stepped-back design by [[Eliel Saarinen]], also proved highly influential.<ref name="Solomonson 2005 147"/>

The popularity of the older style then began to wane in favor of a greater emphasis on towers.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=117}}</ref> One common way of building these within Chicago's laws was to build a square main block with a central service core, and then simply place a tower on the top; the more massive the main block, the taller the tower could be.<ref name=WillisPP118>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=118–119}}</ref> The [[Trustees System Service Building]] and the Foreman State National Bank Building form good examples of this approach.<ref name=WillisPP118/> Alternatively, the front of the main block could be recessed, as at the [[Civic Opera House|Chicago Civic Opera Building]] or the [[LaSalle-Wacker Building]], sacrificing volume but producing the visual effect of two high wings flanking a very tall tower.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=120–121}}</ref> The distinctive New York "setback" style was not adopted in Chicago, the only example of this style being the [[Palmolive Building]] on North Michigan Avenue.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=125}}</ref>

===Great Depression===
[[File:Empire State Building by David Shankbone.jpg|thumb|The [[Empire State Building]] in 2007|alt=A view of the Empire State Building from its narrow aspect]]
The boom in skyscraper construction began to falter following the [[Wall Street crash of 1929]], with fast economic growth giving way to the slump years of the [[Great Depression]]: construction of all sorts slowed considerably.<ref name="Shepherd 2003 226">{{harvnb|Shepherd|2003|p=226}}</ref> The real estate market that lay behind new skyscraper builds collapsed, and the value of many properties dropped dramatically: the [[LeVeque Tower|American Insurance Union]] tower cost $8 million ($1.2 billion in 2010 terms) to build in 1927, but was valued at only $3.5 million ($900 million) by 1933; 40 Wall Street defaulted on its debts in 1935 and was put on sale for just $1.2 million ($240 m).<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=164}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=41}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=29}}</ref>{{refn|Put on sale for $1.2 million, 40 Wall Street was valued at less than the original cost of its elevators. Skyscraper values during the Depression years should be seen against a context of [[deflation]] and a shrinking economy.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=29}}</ref>|group=nb}} The major bond house of S.W. Straus, behind many successful developments, defaulted on the $214 million ($47 billion) in bonds held by 60,000 investors; the Van Swerigan developer brothers went bankrupt.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=164}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=41}}</ref> Vacancy rates began to increase as the recession bit, increasing from only one percent in central New York in early 1920 to 17 percent in 1931 and 25 percent by 1934.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=165}}</ref>

In the face of the recession, some skyscrapers projects were canceled or scaled back. Plans by the [[MetLife|Metropolitan Life]] company to build a 100-story skyscraper alongside their existing tower had been put forward in 1929, but were shelved in the face of the recession and public criticism of such expenditure in the economic climate.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|pp=137–138}}</ref> Instead the first phase of the project, known as the [[Metropolitan Life North Building|North Building]] ended up only 32 stories high in 1932 and the building, even at this height, was only fully completed in 1950.<ref>{{harvnb|Moudry|2005b|p=138}}</ref> In many other cases, projects which had already been commissioned continued through to completion. This resulted in {{convert|26000000|sqft|m2|sigfig=2}} of new office space being added to New York between 1931 and 1934 even after the start of the recession, adding to the problem of underoccupancy.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=88}}</ref> Some of these buildings, however, became iconic structures, pushing the limits of skyscraper height sharply upwards.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=77}}</ref>

The [[Chrysler Building]] was completed in 1930, just after the Depression began to affect the industry.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=79}}</ref> Architect [[William Van Alen]] competed with the designers of 40 Wall Street to produce the tallest building in the world and famously erected the Chrysler spire in a last-minute, secret move in order to acquire the title for his own 69-story, {{convert|1046|ft|adj=on}} tall building.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|pp=82–83}}; {{harvnb|Douglas|1996|p=96}}</ref> The exterior was built of white and grey brick, but metal was used extensively to ornament it further, including gargoyles, [[nickel]]-[[Chrome plating|chrome]] eagles' heads, and a winged helmet of [[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]].<ref>{{harvnb|Douglas|1996|p=96}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=80}}</ref> The entrance used black granite to contrast with the nickel-chrome windows, and the foyer gave way to red marble and a mural ceiling.<ref>{{harvnb|Douglas|1996|p=97}}</ref> The design of each part of the building was individualist and distinct, with even each elevator different in design.<ref name="Douglas 1996 85"/> A [[Chrysler]] showroom was placed on the first floor of the building and an observation deck and the exclusive "Cloud Club" on the upper levels.<ref>{{harvnb|Douglas|1996|pp=97–97}}</ref>

[[File:Rockefeller Center, December 1933.jpg|thumb|left|The [[construction of Rockefeller Center|construction]] of [[Rockefeller Center]] at night, 1933|alt=A monochrome image of a building being constructed, with lit office rooms especially prominent]]
The [[Empire State Building]] originated from a 1928 project to redevelop the original [[Waldorf–Astoria (1893–1929)|Waldorf–Astoria]] into a 50-story mixed-use development; the purchase of the site for $14 million ($2.1 billion) set a record in New York for the year.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=90}}</ref> [[John J. Raskob|John Raskob]] and [[Pierre S. du Pont|Pierre du Pont]] entered into the project as financial backers, and concluded that the project would be more profitable if the site was used to build an extremely tall 80-story skyscraper instead.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=90–95}}</ref> Although revised financial estimates suggested that the height should be cut back, the cachet of having the world's tallest building was considerable, and instead an additional five stories were added to ensure the building, at {{convert|1050|ft}}, would be slightly taller than the Chrysler Building.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=98–99}}</ref> An observation deck was built to attract tourists, which proved to be a valuable source of revenue.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=100}}</ref> The [[limestone]], [[granite]], and [[aluminium]] skyscraper was specially designed to be easily erected, with standardized paneling and structural fittings, and was completed in only 18 months, opening in 1931.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=100–101}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=85}}</ref> Due to the recession, however, it was only 25 percent occupied throughout the 1930s and ran at a loss; critics dubbed it the "Empty State Building".<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=90}}; {{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=120}}</ref>

[[Rockefeller Center]] had originally been intended by [[John D. Rockefeller Jr.]] to be a new location for the [[Metropolitan Opera House (39th Street)|Metropolitan Opera House]], but the 1929 crash brought an end to the scheme.<ref>{{harvnb|Krinsky|2005|pp=203–204}}</ref> Rockefeller [[Construction of Rockefeller Center|decided to develop a large office center instead]], taking advantage of the low construction costs during the recession.<ref>{{harvnb|Krinsky|2005|pp=202–204, 208}}; {{harvnb|Ford|2005|p=43}}</ref> At the center of the development was the [[30 Rockefeller Plaza|RCA Building]], heavily influenced by architect Raymond Hood.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=103}}</ref> The long, slab-like RCA had two distinct axes – from one side, it appeared to be a narrow tower, from the other it rose like a sheer wall.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=105}}</ref> Not only was the structure highly distinctive, but it was also economically very effective. The design maximized the available light to the offices and eliminated any darker internal rooms, as the core of the building was entirely taken up with elevators and other engineering services.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=106}}</ref> It took until 1940 before all of the building had been filled by tenants.<ref>{{harvnb|Krinsky|2005|p=208}}</ref>

In Chicago, the final pre-war skyscraper was built in 1934.<ref name="Willis 1995 128–129">{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=128–129}}</ref> The [[Field Building (Chicago)|Field Building]] was commissioned during the final boom years of the inter-war economy, and the Home Insurance Building – the first skyscraper, built in 1884 – was demolished to make way for the "wing and tower"-style development.<ref name="Willis 1995 128–129"/>

===Skyscraper mania and social commentary===
[[File:Construction old and new from 37 Washington Street, New York City (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Berenice Abbott]]'s depiction of changing Manhattan, 1936; [[Cunard Building (New York City)|Cunard Building]] (right)|alt=Old tenements with laundry from clotheslines are contrasted with imposing new skyscrapers]]
Public interest in skyscrapers increased during the 1920s, particularly after the Tribune competition.<ref name=SchleierP70>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=70}}</ref> The competition drawings were circulated on display, with 25,000 people coming to see them in Chicago in just one month.<ref name=SchleierP71>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=71}}</ref> In the aftermath, images of skyscrapers flourished across American culture, commencing what historian Merrill Schleier dubbed a "skyscraper mania".<ref name="Schleier 1986 69"/> The "Titan City" exhibition in 1925 celebrated existing skyscraper and featured futuristic murals by [[Harvey Wiley Corbett|Harvey Corbett]] and [[Hugh Ferriss]], depicting the skyscraper at the heart of the "City of the Future".<ref name=SchleierP70/> [[Charles Sheeler]] and [[Paul Strand]]'s 1921 short film ''[[Manhatta]]'' explored the form, ending with a sunset shot from the top of a skyscraper.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=79}}</ref> Authors such as [[Janet Flanner]], [[John Dos Passos]] and [[Mary Borden]] wrote novels with skyscrapers as important motifs or settings.<ref name=SchleierP71/> [[John Alden Carpenter|John Carpenter]] produced a [[ballet]] on the theme.<ref name=SchleierP71/> [[Paul T. Frankl|Paul Frankl]] designed a range of popular "skyscraper furniture".<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=11}}</ref>

Much of this commentary was positive, reflecting an optimism about technology and the direction of urban life in general.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|pp=72–73}}</ref> Skyscrapers were seen as an expression of rational engineering, the perfect buildings for mankind to live in, as celebrated in artist [[Louis Lozowick]]'s [[lithograph]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|pp=76–77}}; {{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=177}}</ref> Some other proponents of skyscrapers likened them to medieval cathedrals, symbols of the modern age.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=77}}</ref> Poems depicted skyscrapers as objects of sublime, rational beauty, Ferris describing them as "buildings like crystals, walls of translucent glass, sheer glass blocks sheathing a steel grill".<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=88}}</ref> At Chicago's [[Century of Progress]] exposition in 1933, skyscrapers and technology were portrayed as a solution for the United States' current and future problems.<ref name="Shepherd 2003 226"/> The French-Swiss architect [[Le Corbusier]] acclaimed New York in 1935 as being "overwhelming, amazing, exciting, violently alive", but went on to complain that there were still too few skyscrapers, and those that had been built were not yet tall enough.<ref>{{harvnb|Le Corbusier|1947|p=45}} cited {{harvnb|Page|2005|p=181}}</ref> [[Lewis Hine]], employed to record the building of the Empire State Building, portrayed the skyscraper construction teams as courageous heroes, creating a genre of photography that continued up until 1941.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=121}}</ref>

[[File:Old timer structural worker2.jpg|thumb|left|A worker constructing the [[Empire State Building]] in 1930, overlooking the [[Chrysler Building]] in the background, by [[Lewis Hine]]|alt=A man is working on an I-Beam while the Chrysler Building is seen in the background at right]]
Their critics expressed concerns about the effect of modern technology and urban living on the human condition, arguing that skyscrapers generated pollution and noise, and imposed a regimented and dehumanising lifestyle on the people that worked in them.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|pp=72, 94–95}}</ref> Social commentator [[Lewis Mumford]] reflected the concerns of many in his critiques entitled ''Is the Skyscraper Tolerable?'' and ''The Intolerable City''.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=93}}</ref> Political theorist [[Stefan Hirsch]] condemned the buildings as "bandages covering the sky, stifling our breath".<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|1986|p=103}}</ref> Inventor [[Thomas Edison]] expressed fears that an uncontrolled expansion of skyscrapers would result in overcrowding and disaster.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=88}}</ref> Artist [[Howard Cook]]'s engravings critiqued the oppressive character of the new skyscrapers as they loomed over the traditional city.<ref>{{harvnb|Abramson|2001|p=172}}</ref> [[Berenice Abbott]]'s photographic studies of New York in the 1930s explored the complex theme of urban change and the effect of skyscrapers on the older ways of life in the city, echoing Steigler's work in the first decade of the century.<ref>{{harvnb|Page|2005|pp=165–167}}</ref>

Hollywood used skyscrapers extensively in popular films. ''The Skyscrapers of New York'' in 1906 became the first of many, and in the 1920s [[Harold Lloyd]] produced his five "skyscraper films", most prominently ''[[Safety Last!]]'', in which the hero dangles from a clock on the side of a Los Angeles building.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|2009|pp=2–4}}</ref> In these early [[silent film|silent movies]], skyscrapers were closely associated with masculine identity; Lloyd's climbing of skyscrapers closely associated with his characters' transformation from young men into mature adults, and the winning of the heroine.<ref>{{harvnb|Schleier|2009|pp=3–4, 13}}</ref> The 1933 film [[King Kong (1933 film)|''King Kong'']] included another iconic use of the early skyscraper in its final scenes, as the giant ape scaled the Empire State Building shortly before his death; the scene can be interpreted as contrasting natural instinct with the insensitive rationality of the modern building and wider New York.<ref>{{harvnb|Ramirez|2004|p=175}}</ref>

==Legacy==
[[File:90 West Street Building.jpg|thumb|The [[West Street Building]] in 1988, overshadowed by the modernist [[World Trade Center (1973–2001)|World Trade Center]]|alt=An Italianate building is seen at a 3/4 view, while the bottom half of the pre-2001 World Trade Center towers loom behind it]]
Skyscraper development paused during the years of [[World War II]]. Once development began again in the 1950s and 1960s, the skyscraper entered a different phase of development, usually called the [[International style (architecture)|international]] or [[Modern architecture|modern]] period. Some experimental designs in this style had been built in the U.S. using European architectural concepts in the early 1930s, most notably the [[Loews Philadelphia Hotel|Philadelphia Savings Fund Society]] and [[330 West 42nd Street|McGraw-Hill Building]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Watkin|2005|p=581}}</ref> Post-war, their modernist themes were used in a new generation of skyscrapers. These stood alone on individual plots in the fashion of the Rockefeller Centre's RCA building, rather than as part of a row of buildings, forming huge slabs and towers featuring [[Curtain wall (architecture)|huge glass façades]], breaking with the earlier, more ornate skyscraper traditions.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=134}}; {{harvnb|Goldberger|1985|p=101}}</ref> Inside, new technologies such as [[Fluorescent lamp|fluorescent lighting]] and widespread air-conditioning meant that many older architectural features such as light courts and operable windows were unnecessary.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=132–134}}</ref>

The trend had substantial implications for many early skyscrapers. Some were redesigned to fit new tastes. Much of the ornate detail was removed from the [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower|Metropolitan Life Tower]] in the 1960s, for example, to fit contemporary, plainer fashions.<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=361}}</ref> Many older skyscrapers could not be adapted, however, as they lacked the physical depth to build larger modern offices or the space for new service facilities.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=136}}</ref> A few were demolished to make way for new, larger structures. Notable these was the [[Singer Building|Singer Tower]], razed between 1967 and 1969 and replaced by the international style [[One Liberty Plaza|United States Steel Building]].<ref>{{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=366}}</ref> In the 21st century, buildings such as [[90 West Street]] have been renovated as upmarket housing, because of their large windows in part and aesthetic quality.<ref name=NYT2004>{{cite web| title = 9/11's Miracle Survivor Sheds Bandages: a 1907 Landmark Will be Restored for Residential Use| work = The New York Times| author = Glenn Collins| year = 2004| url = https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/05/nyregion/9-11-s-miracle-survivor-sheds-bandages-1907-landmark-will-be-restored-for.html?pagewanted=3&src=pm. | access-date = September 8, 2012}}</ref>

Critical discussion of early skyscrapers began from the 1880s onwards in the architectural community and continued across a growing cultural and academic community in the inter-war period. In 1930, the terms the [[Chicago school (architecture)|Chicago "school"]] and "movement" began to be used for the first time, popularised by the 1940s academics [[Sigfried Giedion]] and [[Carl W. Condit|Carl Condit]] as a label for the early Chicago architects. They regarded skyscrapers as the early forerunners of modernism and as marking a clear break with earlier architectural forms in the U.S.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|p=11}}; {{harvnb|Bruegmann|1997|p=141}}</ref> This interpretation of Chicago's skyscrapers was later challenged by [[Robert Bruegmann]] and Daniel Bluestone, who argued that it underplayed the links of the movement to pre-existing Chicago culture.<ref name="Willis 1995 11"/> During the 1980s and 1990s, analysis of the early skyscrapers increasingly shifted away from the architects and architecture of the individual buildings to considerations of skyscrapers' roles in the wider urban context.<ref>{{harvnb|Ford|2005|pp=2–3}}</ref> Histories stressing the social, economic, and cultural dimension of skyscrapers began to be produced, with New York's skyscrapers receiving greater attention than before.<ref>{{harvnb|Willis|1995|pp=7–9}}; {{harvnb|Moudry|2005a|p=3}}; {{harvnb|Landau|Condit|1996|p=ix}}</ref> The [[Skyscraper Museum]] – the first to address the theme – was founded in New York in 1997 by historian Carol Willis to preserve the history of the skyscraper.<ref>{{cite web| title = History| publisher = The Skyscraper Museum| year = 2011| url = http://www.skyscraper.org/LOCATION/HISTORY/history.htm | access-date = September 8, 2012}}</ref>
