'''Florence Cathedral''' ({{langx|it|Duomo di Firenze}}), formally the '''Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Flower''' ({{langx|it|Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore|links=no}} {{IPA|it|katteˈdraːle di ˈsanta maˈriːa del ˈfjoːre|}}), is the [[cathedral]] of the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Florence|Catholic Archdiocese of Florence]] in [[Florence|Florence, Italy]]. Commenced in 1296 in the [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] style to a design of [[Arnolfo di Cambio]] and completed by 1436 with a dome engineered by [[Filippo Brunelleschi]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Duomo di Firenze, Florence |url=http://www.aviewoncities.com/florence/duomo.htm |website=A View On Cities |access-date=5 February 2016 |language=en-us |first=Kristiaan Van |last=Ermengem |archive-date=19 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191019100255/http://www.aviewoncities.com/florence/duomo.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> the [[basilica]]'s exterior is faced with [[polychrome]] marble [[Wall panel|panels]] in various shades of green and pink, alternated by white, and features an elaborate 19th-century [[Gothic Revival]] western [[façade]] by [[Emilio De Fabris]].

The cathedral complex, in [[Piazza del Duomo, Florence|Piazza del Duomo]], includes the [[Florence Baptistery]] and [[Giotto's Campanile]]. These three buildings are part of the [[UNESCO World Heritage Site]] covering the [[historic centre of Florence]] and are a major tourist attraction of [[Tuscany]]. The basilica is one of world's largest churches and its dome is still the largest [[masonry]] dome ever constructed.<ref>{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}} (What does it mean: to be one of the world's largest churches? Is it e.g. highest/largest footprint/biggest volume/most seats? Is there a reference of large churches that provides context?)</ref><ref>{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}</ref> The cathedral is the mother church and seat of the Archdiocese of Florence, whose archbishop is [[Gherardo Gambelli]].<ref name="Gambassi2024">{{cite news |last1=Gambassi |first1=Giacomo |title=La nomina. Chi è don Gambelli, il parroco missionario nuovo arcivescovo di Firenze |url=https://www.avvenire.it/chiesa/pagine/don-gherardo-gambelli-nuovo-arcivescovo-firenze |access-date=26 October 2024 |work=www.avvenire.it |date=19 April 2024}}</ref>

[[File:Façade cathédrale Florence.jpg|thumb|The 19th century [[Gothic Revival|Neo-Gothic]] façade]]

==History==
Santa Maria del Fiore was built on the site of Florence's second cathedral dedicated to [[Saint Reparata]];<ref name="bartlett 36 37">Bartlett, pp. 36–37; according to Bartlett, the people of Florence continued to call the cathedral by its former name for some time after reconstruction.</ref> the first bishop's seat was the [[San Lorenzo, Florence|Basilica of San Lorenzo]], the initial building of which was consecrated as a church in 393 by [[St. Ambrose of Milan]].<ref name="Paoletti/Radke">{{cite book|author1=Paoletti, John T. |author2=Gary M. Radke |date=2011 |orig-date=1997 |title=Art in Renaissance Italy |edition=4 |location=London |publisher=Lawrence King |page=250f |isbn=978-1-85669-797-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.haber46.com.tr/guncel/michelangelo-ronesans-doneminde-floransanin-onde-gelen-medici-ailesinin-h343075.html |title=Michelangelo Rönesans döneminde Floransanın önde gelen Medici Ailesinin özel bir isteği üzerine hangisini yapmıştır |first=Güncelleme |last=Tarihi |date=23 May 2018 |access-date=5 July 2018 |work=Haber46 |language=tr |archive-date=5 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180705121439/https://www.haber46.com.tr/guncel/michelangelo-ronesans-doneminde-floransanin-onde-gelen-medici-ailesinin-h343075.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The ancient structure, founded in the early 5th century and having undergone many repairs, was crumbling with age, according to the 14th-century ''[[Nuova Cronica]]'' of [[Giovanni Villani]],<ref name="bartlett 36">Barlett, 36.</ref> and was no longer large enough to serve the growing population of the city.<ref name="bartlett 36" /> Other major Tuscan cities had undertaken ambitious reconstructions of their cathedrals during the Late Medieval period, such as [[Pisa Cathedral|Pisa]] and particularly [[Siena Cathedral|Siena]] where enormous proposed extensions were never completed.

[[File:Codice rustici, santa maria del fiore.jpg|thumb|The Cathedral as depicted in the ''Codex Rustici'' of 1447]]

The city council of Florence approved [[Arnolfo di Cambio]]'s design for the new church in 1294.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Margaret |last=Haines |title=Brunelleschi and Bureaucracy: The Tradition of Public Patronage at the Florentine Cathedral |journal=I Tatti Studies in the Italian Renaissance |volume=3 |year=1989 |pages=89–115 |doi=10.2307/4603662 |jstor=4603662 |s2cid=159633596 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2S0rnQEACAAJ |access-date=20 August 2019 |archive-date=26 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191226103927/https://books.google.com/books?id=2S0rnQEACAAJ |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Di Cambio was also architect of the church of [[Basilica di Santa Croce di Firenze|Santa Croce]] and the [[Palazzo Vecchio]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wga.hu/html_m/a/arnolfo/7/croce2.html |title=View of the nave and choir by Arnolfo di Cambio |first1=Emil |last1=Krén |first2=Daniel |last2=Marx |access-date=5 July 2018 |work=[[Web Gallery of Art]] |archive-date=26 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191226103930/https://www.wga.hu/html_m/a/arnolfo/7/croce2.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.italoamericano.org/story/2017-1-11/medici-palazzo-vecchio |title=Inside the House of Medici (Part II): Palazzo Vecchio |last=Sannio |first=Simone |date=12 January 2017 |access-date=5 July 2017 |newspaper=L'Italo-Americano |archive-date=7 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200207005430/https://italoamericano.org/story/2017-1-11/medici-palazzo-vecchio |url-status=dead}}</ref> He designed three wide [[nave|naves]] ending under an octagonal dome, with the middle nave covering the area of Santa Reparata. The first stone was laid on 9 September 1296, by Cardinal Valeriana, the first [[papal legate]] ever sent to Florence. The building of this vast project was to last 140 years; Arnolfo's plan for the eastern end, although maintained in concept, was greatly expanded in size.

[[File:Andrea di bonaiuto, dettaglio dal cappoellone degli spagnoli.jpg|thumb|The ''Duomo,'' as if completed, in a [[fresco]] by [[Andrea di Bonaiuto]], painted in the 1360s, before the commencement of the dome]]

After Arnolfo died in 1302, building of the cathedral slowed for almost 50 years. When the relics of [[Saint Zenobius]] were discovered in 1330 in Santa Reparata, the project gained a new impetus. In 1331, the ''[[Arte della Lana]],'' the [[Guilds of Florence|guild of wool merchants]], took over patronage for the construction of the cathedral and in 1334 appointed [[Giotto di Bondone|Giotto]] to oversee the work. Assisted by [[Andrea Pisano]], Giotto continued di Cambio's design. His major contribution was to design and begin the construction of the ''[[campanile]].'' When Giotto died on 8 January 1337, Andrea Pisano continued the building until work was halted due to the [[Black Death]] in 1348.

In 1349, action resumed on the cathedral under a series of architects, starting with [[Francesco Talenti]], who finished the ''campanile'' and enlarged the overall project to include the [[apse]] and the side chapels. In 1359, Talenti was succeeded by [[Giovanni di Lapo Ghini]] (1360–1369) who divided the centre nave into four square bays. Other architects were [[Alberto Arnoldi]], Giovanni d'Ambrogio, Neri di Fioravanti and [[Andrea Orcagna]]. By 1375, the old church of Santa Reparata was pulled down. The nave was finished by 1380, and only the dome remained incomplete until 1436.

On 19 August 1418,<ref>{{Cite book |title=Brunelleschi's Dome: How a Renaissance Genius Reinvented Architecture |last=King |first=Ross |publisher=Bloomsbury |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8027-1366-7 |location=New York |pages=1}}</ref> the ''Arte della Lana'' announced an [[architectural design competition]] for erecting Neri's dome. The two main competitors were two master goldsmiths, [[Lorenzo Ghiberti]] and [[Filippo Brunelleschi]], the latter of whom was supported by [[Cosimo de' Medici]]. Ghiberti had been the winner of a competition for a [[North Doors of the Florence Baptistery|pair of bronze doors]] for the [[Florence Baptistery|Baptistery]] in 1401 and lifelong competition between the two seem to remain. Brunelleschi won and received the commission.<ref name=arch>{{cite book |first=Guido |last=Zucconi |year=1995 |title=Florence: An Architectural Guide |publisher=Arsenale Editrice srl |location=San Giovanni Lupatoto, Vr, Italy |isbn=978-88-7743-147-9}}</ref>

Ghiberti, appointed coadjutor, drew a salary equal to Brunelleschi's and, though neither was awarded the announced prize of 200 florins, was promised equal credit, although he spent most of his time on other projects. When Brunelleschi became ill, or feigned illness, the project was briefly in the hands of Ghiberti, but soon he supposedly had to admit that the whole project was beyond him. In 1423, Brunelleschi was back in charge and took over sole responsibility.<ref>King, pp. 76–79.</ref>

Erection of the dome had begun in 1420 and was finished in 1436. The cathedral was consecrated by [[Pope Eugene IV]] on 25 March 1436, the first day of the year according to the Florentine calendar. It was the first 'octagonal dome in history to be built without a temporary wooden supporting frame. During the consecration in 1436, [[Guillaume Dufay]]'s motet ''[[Nuper rosarum flores]]'' was performed.

The decoration of the exterior of the cathedral, begun in the 14th century, was left unfinished after the initial works done by Arnolfo di Cambio, which led Lorenzo de' Medici to initiate a design competition for the façade between 1490 and 1491.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Waldman |first=Louis Alexander |date=1996 |title=Florence Cathedral: The Facade Competition of 1476 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23204946 |journal=Source: Notes in the History of Art |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.1086/sou.16.1.23204946 |jstor=23204946 |issn=0737-4453|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The competition went ultimately nowhere, and the façade wasn't installed until the 19th century, in 1887, with the fabrication of Emilio De Fabris' polychrome marble design. The floor of the church had been relaid in marble tiles in the 16th century.

[[File:Florence Cathedral Santa Maria del Fiore, Porta della Mandorla, relief by Nanni di Banco, 1414–21.jpg|thumb|The ''Madonna of the Girdle'' of the ''Porta della Mandorla'', by [[Nanni di Banco]], 1414–21]]

The exterior walls are faced in alternate vertical and horizontal bands of polychrome marble from [[Carrara]] (white), [[Prato]] (green), [[Siena]] (red), Lavenza and a few other places. De Fabris had to copy the initially [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque]] cladding style peculiar to [[Tuscan order|Tuscan]] church architecture such as <!--of ?-->the earlier [[baptistery]] ([[Battistero di San Giovanni (Florence)|Battistero di San Giovanni]]), and [[Giotto's Bell Tower|Giotto's bell tower]]. There are two major side doors near the crossing: the ''Porta dei Canonici'' on the south side and the ''Porta di Mandorla'' to the north. The [[mandorla]] with the ''[[Girdle of Thomas|Madonna of the Girdle]]'' surrounded by angels was sculpted by [[Nanni di Banco]]. Nanni who worked with his father and others on the door, died way too early before the portal was completed. Nanni and the befriended young [[Donatello]] provided two youthful prophet figures for the top of the [[pinnacle]]s flanking the portal which are now in the [[Museo dell'Opera del Duomo (Florence)|Museo dell'Opera del Duomo]]. The six side windows, notable for their delicate tracery and ornaments, are separated by pilasters. Only the four windows closest to the [[transept]] admit light; the other two are merely ornamental. The [[clerestory]] windows are round, a common Italian Gothic feature.

==Exterior==

===Plan and structure===
[[File:SMDFplan36.gif|thumb|Plan of the church with various extension phases]]
The cathedral of Florence is built as a basilica, having a wide central nave of four square bays, with an aisle on either side. The chancel and transepts are of identical polygonal plan, separated by two smaller polygonal chapels. The whole plan forms a Latin cross. The nave and aisles are separated by wide pointed Gothic arches resting on composite piers.

Its arrangement of trilobate -three lobe- [[apse]]s was intended to evoke the form of a flower, as a homage to Fiorenza, the "city of flowers".<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 June 2025 |title=The masters: architects and sculptors in the 14th and 15th centuries |url=https://duomo.firenze.it/en/about-us/history/art#:~:text=Torna%20su-,The%20masters%3A%20architects%20and%20sculptors%20in%20the%2014th%20and%2015th,the%20%22City%20of%20Flowers%22. |access-date=30 June 2025 |website=Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore}}</ref>

The dimensions of the building are enormous: building area {{cvt|8,300|m2|0|abbr=off}}, length {{cvt|153|m|ft|abbr=off}}, width {{cvt|38|m|ft|abbr=off}}, width at the [[crossing (architecture)|crossing]] {{cvt|90|m|ft|abbr=off}}. The height of the arches in the aisles is {{cvt|23|m|ft|abbr=off}}. The height of the dome is {{cvt|114.5|m|ft|1|abbr=off}}.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://en.firenze-online.com/visit/informations-florence.php?id=2 |title=Santa Maria Del Fiore Church (Dome) Firenze Italy |publisher=En.firenze-online.com |access-date=26 March 2013 |archive-date=25 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191025001234/http://en.firenze-online.com/visit/informations-florence.php?id=2 |url-status=live }}</ref> It has the fifth [[List of tallest domes in the world|tallest dome in the world]].

===Planned sculpture for the exterior===
The Overseers of the Office of Works of Florence Cathedral, the [[Arte della Lana]], had plans to commission a series of twelve large [[Old Testament]] sculptures for the [[buttress]]es of the cathedral.<ref>Charles Seymour, Jr. "''Homo Magnus et Albus:'' the Quattrocento Background for Michelangelo's ''David'' of 1501–04," ''Stil und Überlieferung in der Kunst des Abendlandes'', Berlin, 1967, II, 96–105.</ref> [[Donatello]], then in his early twenties, was commissioned to carve a statue of David in 1408, to top one of the [[buttress]]es, though it was never placed there. [[Nanni di Banco]] was commissioned to carve a marble statue of [[Isaiah]], at the same scale, in the same year. One of the statues was lifted into place in 1409, but was found to be too small to be easily visible from the ground and was taken down; both statues then languished in the workshop of the ''opera'' for several years.<ref>[[#Janson|Janson]], pp. 3–7</ref><ref>Pope-Hennessey, John (1958) ''Italian Renaissance Sculpture,'' London, pp. 6–7</ref><ref>[[#Poeschke|Poeschke]], p. 27.</ref> <!-- In 1410 [[Donatello]] made the first of the statues, a figure of [[Joshua]] in [[terracotta]]. - what the?--> In 1409–1411 Donatello made a statue of a sitting ''Saint John the Evangelist'' which until 1588 was in a niche of the old cathedral façade. Between 1415 and 1426, Donatello created five statues for the [[Campanile di Giotto|campanile]] of [[Santa Maria del Fiore]]. These are the ''Beardless'' and the ''Bearded Prophet'' (both from 1415); the ''Sacrifice of Isaac'' (1421); ''[[Statue of Habacuc|Habbakuk]]'' (1423–25); and ''Jeremiah'' (1423–26); which follow the classical models for [[orator]]s and are characterised by strong portrait details. A figure of [[Hercules]], <!-- also --> in terracotta, was commissioned from the Florentine sculptor [[Agostino di Duccio]] in 1463 and was made perhaps under Donatello's direction.<ref>Seymour, 100–101.</ref> A statue of David by Michelangelo was completed 1501–1504 although it could not be placed on the buttress because of its six-ton weight. In 2010 a fiberglass replica of "David" was placed for one day on a roof-top buttress for a chapel's dome.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=McCormack |first=Claire |date=2010-11-16 |title=Michelangelo's David, Finally As It Was Always Meant To Be Seen |url=https://newsfeed.time.com/2010/11/16/michelangelos-david-finally-as-it-was-always-meant-to-be-seen/ |access-date=2025-07-06 |magazine=Time |language=en-US |issn=0040-781X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2010-11-19 |title=Michelangelo's David on the Duomo roof – The History Blog |url=https://www.thehistoryblog.com/archives/8533 |access-date=2025-07-06 |language=en-US}}</ref>

<gallery widths=150 heights=200>
File:Donatello, david (marmo) 01.JPG|Donatello first version of ''David'' (1408–09). [[Bargello|Museo Nazionale del Bargello]], [[Florence]]. Height 191&nbsp;cm.
<!-- File:Smf, statua in nicchione 04 isaia by nanni di banco.jpg|Possible Statue of "Isaiah" by Nanni di Banco -->
File:Sangiovannievangelista.jpg|Donatello's colossal seated figure of ''Saint John the Evangelist''; 1409–11
File:David sullo sperone del duomo di firenze 04.JPG|A fiberglass replica of Michaelangelo's ''David'' statue [seen from the north]. This was the original placement planned for the statue.
</gallery>

===Dome===
[[File:Brunelleschi's Dome, Florence Cathedral.jpg|thumb| Close view of the dome]]

After a hundred years of construction and by the beginning of the 15th century, the structure was still missing its [[dome]]. The basic features of the dome had been designed by Arnolfo di Cambio in 1296. His brick model, {{cvt|4.6|m|ft|1|abbr=off}} high, {{cvt|9.2|m|ft|1|abbr=off}} long, was standing in a side aisle of the unfinished building, and had long been sacrosanct.<ref>King, p. 10</ref> It called for an octagonal dome higher and wider than any that had ever been built, with no external buttresses to keep it from spreading and falling under its own weight.
<ref name="smarth">{{cite web |title=Brunelleschi's Dome |publisher=Smarthistory at Khan Academy |url=http://smarthistory.khanacademy.org/brunelleschis-dome.html |access-date=19 December 2012 |archive-date=16 January 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130116124256/http://smarthistory.khanacademy.org/brunelleschis-dome.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The commitment to reject traditional [[Flying buttress|Gothic buttresses]] had been made when Neri di Fioravanti's model was chosen over a competing one by [[Giovanni di Lapo Ghini]].<ref>King, p. 9.</ref> That architectural choice, in 1367, was one of the first events of the Italian [[Renaissance]], marking a break with the [[Gothic architecture#Characteristics of Gothic churches and cathedrals|Medieval Gothic]] style and a return to the classic Mediterranean dome. Italian architects regarded Gothic flying buttresses as ugly makeshifts. Furthermore, the use of buttresses was forbidden in Florence, as the style was favored by central Italy's traditional enemies to the north.<ref>King, p. 7.</ref> Neri's model depicted a massive inner dome, open at the top to admit light, like Rome's [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]], partly supported by the inner dome, but enclosed in a thinner outer shell, to keep out the weather. It was to stand on an unbuttressed octagonal [[Tholobate|drum]]. Neri's dome would need an internal defense against spreading (hoop stress), but none had yet been designed.

The building of such a masonry dome posed many technical problems. Brunelleschi looked to the great dome of the [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]] in Rome for solutions. The dome of the Pantheon is a single shell of concrete, the formula for which had long since been forgotten. The Pantheon had employed structural [[centring]] to support the concrete dome while it cured.<ref>Lancaster, Lynne (2005) Concrete Vaulted Construction in Imperial Rome: Innovations in Context, Cambridge University Press, p. 44</ref> This could not be the solution in the case of a dome this size and would put the church out of use. For the height and breadth of the dome designed by Neri, starting {{cvt|52|m|ft}} above the floor and spanning {{cvt|44|m|ft}}, there was not enough timber in Tuscany to build the scaffolding and forms.<ref>For a fictional impression see PBS' ''The Medici: Godfathers of the Renaissance, Birth of a Dynasty'' (on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9FFDJK8jmms {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170123032955/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9FFDJK8jmms |date=23 January 2017 }} at the 20:15 mark)</ref> Brunelleschi chose to follow such a design and employed a double shell, a form of construction with earlier precedents in Persian and Central Asian architecture.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} Both shells were built of brick, chosen for its light weight compared to stone and the ease of forming it in place, and raised with nothing supporting them from below during construction. Sandstone and marble were reserved for the tension chains, the ribs and the lantern. To illustrate his proposed structural plan, he constructed a wooden and brick model with the help of [[Donatello]] and Nanni di Banco, a model which is still displayed in the [[Museo dell'Opera del Duomo (Florence)|Museo dell'Opera del Duomo]]. The model served as a guide for the craftsmen, but was intentionally incomplete, so as to ensure Brunelleschi's control over the construction.
[[File:Dome of Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore (Florence).jpg|thumb|Interior of the dome]]

Brunelleschi's solutions were ingenious. The spreading problem was solved by a set of four internal horizontal stone and iron chains, serving as barrel hoops, embedded within the inner dome: one at the top, one at the bottom, with the remaining two evenly spaced between them. A fifth chain, made of wood, was placed between the first and second of the stone chains. Since the dome was octagonal rather than round, a simple chain, squeezing the dome like a barrel hoop, would have put all its pressure on the eight corners of the dome. The chains needed to be rigid octagons, stiff enough to hold their shape, so as not to deform the dome as they held it together.<ref name="smarth"/>

Each of Brunelleschi's stone chains was built like an octagonal railroad track with parallel rails and cross ties, all made of sandstone beams {{cvt|43|cm|in}} in diameter and no more than {{cvt|2.3|m|ft}} long. The rails were connected end-to-end with lead-glazed iron splices. The cross ties and rails were notched together and then covered with the bricks and mortar of the inner dome. The cross ties of the bottom chain can be seen protruding from the drum at the base of the dome. The others are hidden. Each stone chain was supposed to be reinforced with a standard iron chain made of interlocking links, but a magnetic survey conducted in the 1970s failed to detect any evidence of iron chains, which if they exist are deeply embedded in the thick masonry walls. Brunelleschi also included vertical "ribs" set on the corners of the octagon, curving towards the center point. The ribs, {{cvt|4|m|ft}} deep, are supported by 16 concealed ribs radiating from center.<ref>Stevenson, Niel (2007) ''Architecture Explained''. {{ISBN|0756628687}}. pp. 36–37.</ref> The ribs had slits to take beams that supported platforms, thus allowing the work to progress upward without the need for scaffolding.<ref>King, pp. 70–73.</ref>

A circular masonry dome can be built without supports, called centering, because each course of bricks is a horizontal arch that resists compression. In Florence, the octagonal inner dome was thick enough for an imaginary circle to be embedded in it at each level, a feature that would hold the dome up eventually, but could not hold the bricks in place while the mortar was still wet. Brunelleschi used a [[Opus spicatum|herringbone brick pattern]] to transfer the weight of the freshly laid bricks to the nearest vertical ribs of the non-circular dome.<ref>King, p. 97.</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Mueller |first=Tom |title=Mystery of Florence's Cathedral Dome May Be Solved |publisher=[[National Geographic Society]] |date=10 February 2014 |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2014/02/140210-duomo-florence-brunelleschi-cathedral-architecture/ |access-date=31 December 2014 |archive-date=30 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190630022212/https://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2014/02/140210-duomo-florence-brunelleschi-cathedral-architecture/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2014/02/il-duomo/mueller-text |title=NationalGeographic.com 2014-02 Il Duomo Tom Mueller |access-date=28 December 2014 |archive-date=25 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160525032445/http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2014/02/il-duomo/mueller-text |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2014/02/il-duomo/design-video |title=NationalGeographic.com 2014-02 Il Doumo Design Video |access-date=12 April 2015 |archive-date=27 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180327213855/http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2014/02/il-duomo/design-video |url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[File:Florence duomo fc02.jpg|thumb|Baptistery of St. John next to the cathedral]]

The outer dome was not thick enough to contain embedded horizontal circles, being only {{cvt|60|cm|ft|0}} thick at the base and {{cvt|30|cm|ft|0}} thick at the top. To create such circles, Brunelleschi thickened the outer dome at the inside of its corners at nine different elevations, creating nine masonry rings, which can be observed today from the space between the two domes. To counteract hoop stress, the outer dome relies entirely on its attachment to the inner dome and has no embedded chains.<ref>King, pp. 105–107.</ref>

A modern understanding of physical laws and the mathematical tools for calculating stresses were centuries in the future. Brunelleschi, like all cathedral builders, had to rely on intuition and whatever he could learn from the large scale models he built. To lift 37,000 [[metric ton|tons]] of material, including over 4 million bricks, he invented hoisting machines and [[lewisson]]s for hoisting large stones. These specially designed machines and his structural innovations were Brunelleschi's chief contribution to architecture. Although he was executing an aesthetic plan made half a century earlier, it is his name, rather than Neri's, that is commonly associated with the dome.

Brunelleschi's ability to crown the dome with a [[cupola|lantern]] was questioned and he had to undergo another competition, even though there had been evidence that Brunelleschi had been working on a design for a lantern for the upper part of the dome. The evidence is shown in the curvature, which was made steeper than the original model.<ref>Gartner, Peter, ''Filippo Brunelleschi 1377–1446'', p 95.</ref> He was declared the winner over his competitors Lorenzo Ghiberti and Antonio Ciaccheri. His design (now on display in the Museum Opera del Duomo) was for an octagonal lantern with eight radiating [[buttress]]es and eight high arched windows. Construction of the lantern was begun a few months before his death in 1446. Then, for 15 years, little progress was possible, due to alterations by several architects. The lantern was finally completed by Brunelleschi's friend [[Michelozzo]] in 1461. The conical roof was crowned with a gilt copper ball and cross, containing holy relics, by [[Verrocchio]] in 1469. This brings the total height of the dome and lantern to {{cvt|114.5|m|ft}}. This copper ball was struck by lightning on 17 July 1600 and fell down. It was replaced by an even larger one two years later.

[[File:Florence duomo fc10.jpg|thumb|Cupola of the Dome]]
[[File:Dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence, Italy.jpg|thumb|Dome from below]]
The commission for this gilt copper ball [atop the lantern] went to the sculptor Andrea del Verrocchio, in whose workshop [[Leonardo da Vinci]] was a young apprentice. Fascinated by Filippo's [Brunelleschi's] machines, which Verrocchio used to hoist the ball, Leonardo made a series of sketches of them and, as a result, is often given credit for their invention.<ref>King, p. 69.</ref> Leonardo might have also participated in the design of the bronze ball, as stated in the G manuscript of Paris "Remember the way we soldered the ball of Santa Maria del Fiore".<ref>Paolo Galluzzi, "Leonard de Vinci, engineer and architect", p. 50</ref>

The decorations of the drum gallery by [[Baccio D'Agnolo|Baccio d'Agnolo]] were never finished after being disapproved of by [[Michelangelo]].{{cn|date=August 2026}}

A statue of Brunelleschi sits outside the Palazzo dei Canonici in the Piazza del Duomo, looking up towards his greatest the dome that has dominated the panorama of Florence. It is still the largest masonry dome in the world.<ref>Figures vary. [http://eng.archinform.net/projekte/939.htm archINFORM] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210620014357/https://ajax.googleapis.com/ajax/libs/jquery/3.6.0/jquery.min.js |date=20 June 2021 }} gives a 45 m wide tambour, while {{Structurae|id=20000294|title=Santa Maria del Fiore}} gives a 43 m diameter of the cupola, others as little as 42 m.</ref>

The building of the cathedral had started in 1296 with the design of Arnolfo di Cambio and was completed in 1469 with the placing of Verrochio's copper ball atop the lantern. The façade was still unfinished and remained so until the 19th century.

===Façade===
The original façade, designed by Arnolfo di Cambio and usually attributed to Giotto, was actually begun twenty years after Giotto's death.{{Citation needed|date=November 2008}} A mid-15th-century pen-and-ink drawing of this so-called Giotto's façade is visible in the [[Codex Rustici]], and in the drawing of [[Bernardino Poccetti]] in 1587, both on display in the Museum of the Opera del Duomo. This façade was the collective work of several artists, among them [[Andrea Orcagna]] and [[Taddeo Gaddi]]. This original façade was completed in only its lower portion and then left unfinished. It was dismantled in 1587–1588 by the Medici court architect [[Bernardo Buontalenti]], ordered by Grand Duke [[Francesco I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany|Francesco I de' Medici]], as it appeared totally outmoded in Renaissance times. Some of the original sculptures are on display in the Museum Opera del Duomo, behind the cathedral. Others are now in the Berlin Museum and in the [[Louvre]].

The competition for a new façade turned into a huge corruption scandal.{{citation needed|date=October 2018}} The wooden model for the façade of Buontalenti is on display in the Museum Opera del Duomo. A few new designs had been proposed in later years, but the models (of Giovanni Antonio Dosio, Giovanni de' Medici with [[Alessandro Pieroni]] and Giambologna) were not accepted. The façade was then left bare until the 19th century.

In 1864, a competition held to design a new façade was won by [[Emilio De Fabris]] (1808–1883) in 1871. Work began in 1876 and was completed in 1887. This neo-gothic façade in white, green and red marble forms a harmonious entity with the cathedral, Giotto's bell tower and the Baptistery.

==Main portal==
The three huge bronze doors date from 1899 to 1903. They are adorned with scenes from the life of the Madonna. The mosaics in the [[lunette]]s above the doors were designed by [[Niccolò Barabino]]. They represent (from left to right): ''Charity among the founders of Florentine philanthropic institutions''; ''Christ enthroned with Mary and John the Baptist''; and ''Florentine artisans, merchants and humanists''. The [[pediment]] above the central portal contains a half-relief by [[Tito Sarrocchi]] of ''Mary enthroned holding a flowered scepter''. [[Giuseppe Cassioli]] sculpted the right-hand door.

On top of the façade is a series of niches with the twelve Apostles with, in the middle, the Madonna with Child. Between the [[rose window]] and the [[tympanum (architecture)|tympanum]], there is a gallery with busts of great Florentine artists.

==Interior==
[[File:Optical illusion on the floor of the Duomo Firenze (61458).jpg|thumb|Perspective illusion on the floor of the cathedral]]
The [[Gothic architecture|Late Gothic]] interior is vast and gives an impression of emptiness. The relative bareness of the church corresponds with the austerity of religious life as practiced by the [[mendicant orders]] founded in the second half of the 12th and at the beginning of the 13th century.

Many decorations in the church have been lost in the course of time, or have been transferred to the [[Museo dell'Opera del Duomo (Florence)|Museo dell' Opera del Duomo]], such as the magnificent [[organ loft|singing lofts]] (''{{lang|it|cantorie}}'') by [[Luca della Robbia]] and [[Donatello]].

As this cathedral was built with funds from the public, some important works of art in this church honour illustrious men and military leaders (''[[Condottiero|condottiere]]'') of Florence, namely a depiction of [[Dante Alighieri|Dante]] and the frescoed [[equestrian statue]]s of [[Sir John Hawkwood]] and [[Niccolò da Tolentino]].<ref name="King2001">{{Cite book |first=Ross |last=King |title=Brunelleschi's Dome: The Story of the Great Cathedral of Florence |location=New York |publisher=Penguin |year=2001 |isbn=0-8027-1366-1 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/brunelleschisdom00king_1}}</ref>

[[Lorenzo Ghiberti]] had a large artistic impact on the cathedral. Ghiberti worked with [[Filippo Brunelleschi]] on the cathedral for eighteen years and had a large number of projects on almost the whole east end. Some of his works are the stained glass designs for the [[oculi]] in the [[Drum (architecture)|drum]], the bronze shrine of [[Zenobius of Florence|Saint Zenobius]] and marble revetments on the outside of the cathedral.

* ''Dante Before the City of Florence'' by [[Domenico di Michelino]] (1465). The fresco depicts [[Dante Alighieri]] with the three settings of the [[Divine Comedy]] alongside an anachronistic depiction of the cathedral.
* ''[[Funerary Monument to Sir John Hawkwood]]'' by [[Paolo Uccello]] (1436). This almost monochrome [[fresco]], [[Transfer of panel paintings|transferred to canvas]] in the 19th century, is painted in ''[[Green earth|terra verde]]'', a pigment closest to the patina of bronze.
* ''[[Equestrian statue of Niccolò da Tolentino]]'' by [[Andrea del Castagno]] (1456). This fresco, transferred on canvas in the 19th century, in the same style as the previous one, is painted to resemble marble. However, it is more richly decorated and gives more the impression of movement. Both frescoes portray the ''[[condottieri]]'' as heroic figures riding triumphantly. Both painters had problems when applying in painting the new [[Perspective (graphical)|rules of perspective]] to foreshortening: instead of a single [[vanishing point]], both applied two separate points, one for the horse and one for the pedestal.
* Busts of [[Giotto]] (by [[Benedetto da Maiano]]), [[Filippo Brunelleschi|Brunelleschi]] (by Buggiano – 1447), [[Marsilio Ficino]], and [[Antonio Squarcialupi]] (a most famous organist). These busts all date from the 15th and the 16th centuries.

Above the main door is the colossal clock face with fresco portraits of four Prophets or Evangelists by Paolo Uccello (1443). This one-handed liturgical clock shows the 24 hours of the ''hora italica'' ("Italian time"), a period of time ending with sunset at 24 hours. This timetable was used until the 18th century. This is one of the few clocks from that time that still exist and are in working order.<ref name="King2001" />

The church is particularly notable for its 44 [[stained glass]] windows, the largest undertaking of this kind in Italy in the 14th and 15th century. The windows in the aisles and in the transept depict saints from the Old and the New Testament, while the circular windows in the drum of the dome or above the entrance depict Christ and Mary. They were made after designs by the greatest Florentine artists of their time, such as Donatello, Lorenzo Ghiberti, Paolo Uccello and Andrea del Castagno.<ref name="King2001" />

''Christ Crowning Mary as Queen'', the stained-glass circular window above the clock, with a rich range of colouring, was designed by [[Gaddo Gaddi]] in the early 14th century.

Donatello designed the stained-glass window (''Coronation of the Virgin'') in the drum of the dome (the only one that can be seen from the nave).

The funeral monument of Antonio d'Orso (1323), bishop of Florence, was made by [[Tino da Camaino]], the most important funeral sculptor of his time.

The monumental crucifix, behind the Bishop's Chair at the high altar, is by [[Benedetto da Maiano]] (1495–1497). The choir enclosure is the work of the famous [[Bartolommeo Bandinelli]]. The ten-paneled bronze doors of the sacristy were made by Luca della Robbia, who has also two glazed [[terracotta]] works inside the sacristy: ''Angel with Candlestick'' and ''Resurrection of Christ''.<ref name="King2001" />

In the back of the middle of the three apses is the altar of [[Saint Zanobius]], first bishop of Florence. Its silver shrine, a masterpiece of Ghiberti, contains the urn with his relics. The central compartment shows us one of his miracles, the reviving of a dead child. Above this shrine is the painting ''Last Supper'' by the lesser-known [[Giovanni Balducci]]. There was also a glass-paste mosaic panel ''The Bust of Saint Zanobius'' by the 16th-century miniaturist [[Monte di Giovanni]], but it is now on display in the Museum Opera del Duomo.<ref name="King2001" />

Many decorations date from the 16th-century patronage of the Grand Dukes, such as the pavement in coloured marble, attributed to Baccio d'Agnolo and Francesco da Sangallo (1520–26). Some pieces of marble from the façade were used, topside down, in the flooring (as was shown by the restoration of the floor after the 1966 flooding).<ref name="King2001" />

The ceiling of the dome is decorated with a representation of ''[[The Last Judgement (Vasari and Zuccari)|The Last Judgment]]''. Originally left whitewashed following its completion it was the Grand Duke [[Cosimo I de' Medici]] who decided to have the ceiling of the dome painted. This enormous work with 3,600&nbsp;metres² (38 750&nbsp;ft²) of painted surface was commenced in 1572 by [[Giorgio Vasari]] and would not be completed until 1579.<ref name="Shulman" /> The upper portion, near the lantern, representing ''The 24 Elders of Apocalypse'' was finished by Vasari before his death in 1574. Federico Zuccari with the assistance of [[Bartolomeo Carducci]], [[Domenico Passignano]] and [[Stefano Pieri]] finished the other portions: (from top to bottom) ''Choirs of Angels''; ''Christ, Mary and Saints''; ''Virtues, Gifts of the Holy Spirit and Beatitudes''; and at the bottom of the cupola: ''Capital Sins and Hell''. These frescoes are considered Zuccari's greatest work. But the quality of the work is uneven because of the input of different artists and the different techniques. Vasari had used ''[[fresco|true fresco]]'', while Zuccari had painted ''[[Fresco-secco|in secco]]''. During the restoration work, which ended in 1995, the entire pictorial cycle of ''The Last Judgment'' was photographed with specially designed equipment and all the information collected in a catalogue. All the restoration information along with reconstructed images of the frescos were stored and managed in the [[Thesaurus florentinus|Thesaurus Florentinus]] computer system.<ref>As referenced in "Cupola di Santa Maria del Fiore: il cantiere di restauro 1980–1995" by [[Cristina Acidini Luchinat]] and Riccardo Dalla Negra published by [[Istituto Poligrafico e Zecca dello Stato]] (Roma) in 1995 ({{ISBN|8824039561}})</ref><ref>[http://www.sbap-fi.beniculturali.it/index.php?it/223/progetti-e-iniziative-culturali Thesaurus Florentinus project page (in Italian)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517094921/http://www.sbap-fi.beniculturali.it/index.php?it%2F223%2Fprogetti-e-iniziative-culturali |date=17 May 2021 }}, ''Soprintendenza ai Beni Architettonici e Paesaggisitici di Firenze, Ministero dei Beni Culturali''</ref>

==Astronomical observations==
[[File:Osservazione del solstizio 21.06.12, fi, 26.JPG|thumb|Observation of the solstice on 21 June 2012]]

In 1475 the Italian astronomer [[Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli]] (who was also a mathematical tutor of Brunelleschi) pierced a hole in the dome at {{convert|91.05|m|ft}} above the pavement to create a meridian line.<ref>{{cite book |last=Heilbron |first=John Lewis |author-link= |date=1990 |title=The Sun in the Church. Cathedrals as Solar Observatories |url= |location= |publisher=Harvard University Press |page=70 |isbn=0674005368}}</ref> The height precluded the installation of a complete meridian line on the floor of the cathedral, but allowed a short section of approximately {{convert|10|m|ft}} to run between the main altar and the north wall of the transept. This allows for observation for around 35 days either side of the summer solstice.

Due to settlement in the building and also movements due to the outside temperature changes, the meridian line had limited astronomical value and fell into disuse until it was restored in 1755 by [[Leonardo Ximenes]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Del vecchio e nuovo gnomone fiorentino e delle osservazioni astronomiche fisiche ed architettoniche fatte nel verificarne la costruzione |volume=|publisher=Stamperia Imperiale|location=Firenze|year=1757|language=it|url=https://gutenberg.beic.it/webclient/DeliveryManager?pid=12799091}}</ref>

The meridian line was covered over by the ''fabbricieri'' in 1894 and unveiled again in 1997. A yearly re-enactment of the observation takes place on 21 June each year at 12:00 UT.

==Crypt==
[[File:Duomo Firenze Apr 2008 (13).JPG|thumb|upright|Tomb of [[Filippo Brunelleschi]]]]

The cathedral underwent difficult excavations between 1965 and 1974. The archaeological history of this huge area was reconstructed through the work of [[Franklin Toker]]: remains of Roman houses, an early Christian pavement, ruins of the former cathedral of Santa Reparata and successive enlargements of this church. Close to the entrance, in the part of the crypt open to the public, is the tomb of Brunelleschi. While its location is prominent, the actual tomb is simple and humble.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}}

==Cracking of the dome==
[[File:Florence Cathedral seen from Piazzale Michelangelo night dllu.jpg|thumb|The cathedral at night from [[Piazzale Michelangelo]]]]
The unreinforced masonry that Brunelleschi used to construct the dome is weak in tension which leads to cracking when tensile stresses exceed the limited masonry tensile strength. The material is especially susceptible to damage from seismic loading due to its heterogeneity and many surfaces between different materials (stones to mortar connection).<ref name=Souza>{{cite conference |last=Souza |first=Kelsey |title=Evolution of Structural Design and Potential Design Changes |book-title=Proceedings of the Workshop on the Structural Cracking of the Cupola of Santa Maria del Fiore |pages=54–55 |publisher=Los Alamos National Laboratory |date=11 September 2014 |location=Los Alamos, New Mexico |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088 |conference= |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011445/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088_Proceedings_of_the_Workshop_on_the_Structural_Cracking_of_the_Cupola_of_Santa_Maria_del_Fiore |url-status=live }}</ref>

Cracking of the dome was observed even before its construction was completed. It is possible that the first cracks were caused by a strong earthquake in 1453.<ref name=OCE>{{cite journal |last1=Ottoni |first1=Federica |last2=Coïsson |first2=Eva |last3=Blasi |first3=Carlo |title=The Crack Pattern in Brunelleschi's Dome in Florence: Damage Evolution from Historical to Modern Monitoring System Analysis |journal=Advanced Materials Research |volume=133–134 |pages=53–64 |publisher=Trans Tech Publications |place=Switzerland |year=2010 |doi=10.4028/www.scientific.net/AMR.133-134.53 |s2cid=110287028 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272627028 |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011444/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272627028_The_Crack_Pattern_in_Brunelleschi%27s_Dome_in_Florence_Damage_Evolution_from_Historical_to_Modern_Monitoring_System_Analysis |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The first written evidence about the presence of cracks appears in a report by Gherardo Silvani report dated 18 September 1639 which refers to "peli" ("hairs").<ref name=OCE/> In 1694 Giambattista Nelli and Vincenzo Viviani surveyed the cracks with Nelli recording that there were two major cracks with a maximum width of {{cvt|29|mm|in}}.<ref name=OCE/> They believed that the cracks were caused by the weight of the dome, and the resulting horizontal thrusts on the pillars. A commission, headed by Vincenzo Viviani, carried out investigations in 1695 and came to the conclusion that the cracking was due to the dead weight of the buildings. It was proposed that the dome be strengthened by installing four large iron belts; three on the outside of the dome between the bulging area of the dome and the circular windows, while the fourth would be installed internally in the second walkway between the two shells.<ref name=CCG1>{{cite journal |last1=Castoldi |first1=A. |last2=Chiarugi |first2=Andrea |last3=Giuseppetti |first3=G. |last4=Fanelli |first4=A. |last5=Petnni |first5=G. |title=Diagnosis and strengthening of the Brunelleschi Dome |journal=IABSE Reports |volume=70 |pages=440–448 |publisher=ETH-Bibliothek |place=Zurich |year=1993 |url=https://www.e-periodica.ch/cntmng?pid=bse-re-003:1993:70::524 |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=3 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211203033551/https://www.e-periodica.ch/cntmng?pid=bse-re-003:1993:70::524 |url-status=live }}</ref> This was similar to what had been done on the dome of St. Peter's in Rome. After a long debate, a decision was made to leave the dome as it was.<ref name=Montalbano/>

The first most complete survey of the cracks was published in 1757 by the Jesuit Leonardo Ximenes (1716–1786). In his document he described 13 different crack typologies.<ref name=OCE/><ref name=BBB>{{cite book |last1=Borri |first1=Claudio |last2=Betti |first2=Michele |last3=Bartol |first3=Gianni |date=2010 |chapter=Brunelleschi's dome in Florence: The masterpiece of a genius |editor1-last=Zingoni |editor1-first=Alphose |title=Advances and Trends in Structural Engineering, Mechanics and Computation |url=https://www.academia.edu/29045823 |type=Hardback |location=Boca Raton, Florida |publisher=CRC Press |pages=1317–1320 |isbn=978-0-415-58472-2 |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011443/https://www.academia.edu/29045823 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1934, Pier Luigi Nervi, who was head of a special commission established by the Opera del Duomo to study the cracking, observed that the cracks opened and closed with the seasons. In the winter, the dome's stone and bricks would contract causing the cracks to widen, while over the summer the materials would expand and the cracks would close up. While modern buildings by design incorporate expansion joints, the cathedral's dome does not include any and so subsequently developed its own expansion joints in the form of these cracks which allowed the structure to "breathe". To date they have not caused any catastrophic damage to the dome.<ref name=Suro>{{Cite news |last=Suro |first=Roberto |title=Cracks in a Great Dome in Florence May Point to Impending Disaster |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=28 July 1987 |page=C3 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/28/science/cracks-in-a-great-dome-in-florence-may-point-to-impending-disaster.html |access-date=26 February 2010 |archive-date=26 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526211146/http://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/28/science/cracks-in-a-great-dome-in-florence-may-point-to-impending-disaster.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1955 the Opera del Duomo installed 22 mechanical deformometers, which were read four times a year to record the variations in the width of the major cracks in the inner dome. At the same time the dome's internal and external temperatures were also recorded. This remained in service until 2009.<ref name=Ottoni>{{cite conference |last=Ottoni |first=Federica |title=Santa Maria del Fiore Dome: Crack Patten and Monitoring Systems |book-title=Proceedings of the Workshop on the Structural Cracking of the Cupola of Santa Maria del Fiore |pages=25–27 |publisher=Los Alamos National Laboratory |date=11 September 2014 |location=Los Alamos, New Mexico |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088 |conference= |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011445/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088_Proceedings_of_the_Workshop_on_the_Structural_Cracking_of_the_Cupola_of_Santa_Maria_del_Fiore |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1975 a commission was appointed by the Italian government to safeguard the dome.<ref name=Montalbano>{{cite news |last=Montalbano |first=William D. |title=Piazza, Duomo Work: In Florence, It's Politics vs. Preservation |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=21 January 1988 |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-01-21-mn-37484-story.html |accessdate=20 November 2021 |archive-date=3 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211203033550/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-01-21-mn-37484-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1978 a government culture agency decided to restore the frescoes. Brunelleschi left forty eight {{cvt|600|mm|in}} holes in the base of the dome.<ref name=Suro/> They are open on the inside and covered by the outer skin of the dome. It has long been assumed that the holes simply served as mounts for the scaffold used when frescoes were painted on the inside of the dome. While the holes had been able to support the scaffolding used for the creation of the frescos on the interior of the dome they were not strong enough for the network of modern metal scaffolding necessary to provide access for the restoration work undertaken on the frescos between 1979 and 1995. To strengthen the scaffolding, the private company contracted to build scaffolding for the work was allowed in 1982 to fill the holes with concrete so that steel beams could be anchored in them.<ref name=Montalbano/><ref name=Shulman >{{cite web |last=Shulman |first=Ken |title=ART: On the Scaffolds, a Delicate Labor in the Duomo |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=3 December 1989 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/03/arts/art-on-the-scaffolds-a-delicate-labor-in-the-duomo.html |access-date=28 November 2021 |archive-date=3 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211203033550/https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/03/arts/art-on-the-scaffolds-a-delicate-labor-in-the-duomo.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1985 local architect [[Lando Bartoli]] noticed that additional cracks were forming around the sealed holes. It was theorized at the time that in summer the four major masses separated by the "A" cracks expanded into the fissures, but now, at the base of the dome, the masses come up against the unyielding concrete that now fills the 48 holes acts as a fulcrum which causes the energy that was once dissipated with the closing of the fissures and into the holes to be transferred into the upper areas of the dome.<ref name=Suro/><ref name=Shulman/>
However analysis by Andrea Chiarugi, Michele Fanelli and Giuseppetti (published in 1983) found that the principal source of the cracks was a dead-weight effect due to the geometry of the dome, its weight (estimated to be 25,000 tons)<ref name=Shulman/> and the insufficient resistance of the ring beam, while thermal variations, has caused fatigue loading and thus expanding of the structure.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Chiarugi |first1=Andrea |last2=Fanelli |first2=Michele |last3=Giuseppetti |first3=G. |title=Analysis of a Brunelleschi-Type Dome Including Thermal Loads |book-title=Proceeding of IABSE Symposium on Strengthening of Building Structure, Diagnosis and Therapy |pages=169–178 |publisher= |date=1983 |location=Zurich}}</ref><ref name=Souza/>
This is a well-known collapse mechanism typical of domed structures: a lowering of the top of the structure under its own weight with significant horizontal thrusts on the bearing elements.<ref name=Ottoni/>

In 1985 a commission established by the Italian Ministry of Cultural and Monumental Heritage accepted this theory.<ref name=CCG1/><ref name=BBB/> The debate about the filling of the scaffolding holes was finally settled in 1987 when it was demonstrated that closing the 48 holes had had no impact on the expansion and contraction of the dome.<ref name=Shulman/> A survey completed in 1984 counted a total of 493 cracks of various sizes, sorted into categories identified by the letters "A" through "D".<ref name=Suro/> These are as follows:
*Type A. These are sub-vertical major cracks that start from the ring beam and continue upwards for approximately two-thirds of the height of the dome; they pass through both the internal and external layer of the even webs and their range in thickness from {{cvt|55|mm|in}} to {{cvt|60|mm|in}} (webs 4 and 6) and {{cvt|25|mm|in}} to {{cvt|30|mm|in}} (webs 2 and 8).<ref name=BBB/> The dome has eight webs numbered counter clockwise from 1, which faces the main nave of the cathedral. These effectively divide the dome into quarters and never completely close in summer.<ref name=Suro/> There is a theory that the plaster used to patch the cracks over the years and crumbling building materials have jammed the fissures.<ref name=Suro/>
*Type B. These sub-vertical minor cracks are located near the circular windows.<ref name=BBB/>
*Type C.  These are sub-vertical minor cracks that are present around the eight edges of the dome.<ref name=BBB/>
*Type D . These are four sub-vertical minor cracks in the internal part of the odd webs. They do not pass through the width of the dome.<ref name=BBB/>
All have formed in a symmetrical pattern.

The development of  the Type "A"  cracks means that the dome now permanently behaves as four drifting half-arches linked below the upper [[Oculus (architecture)|oculus]].<ref name=BBB/> The abutments of these half-arches are constituted by the pillars,  the chapels and the nave of the church. The differences in the cracking patterns between even and odd webs is believed to be due to variations in the stiffness of the supporting ring beam structure under the dome as it is supported by four heavy pillars which line up with the even webs while the odd webs are located over four arches which connect the  pillars.<ref name=BBB/>

In 1987 a second, more comprehensive digital system (which automatically collects data every six hours) was installed by ISMES (in cooperation with the ''Soprintendenza'', the local branch of the [[Ministry of Culture (Italy)|Ministry of Culture]], which is responsible for the conservation of all historical monuments in Florence). It consists of 166 instruments, among which are 60 thermometers measuring the masonry and air temperature  at various locations, 72 inductive type displacement [[transducer]]s (deformometers) at various levels on the main cracks of the inner and outer domes; eight plumb-lines at the centre of each web, which measure the relative displacements between pillars and [[tambour]]; eight livellometers and two [[piezometer]]s, one near the web 4 and the other below the nave which register the variation of the underground water level.<ref name=Ottoni/> A linear regression analysis of the recorded data has shown that the major cracks are widening by approximately   {{cvt|3|mm|in}} per century.<ref name=Ottoni/><ref name=OCE/> Another source quotes a movement of 5.5mm.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Como |first=Mario |title=Brunelleschi's Dome: A New Estimate of the Thrust and Stresses in the Underlying Piers |journal=Applied Sciences |volume=11 |issue=4268 |publisher=MDPI |year=2021 |page=4268 |doi=10.3390/app11094268 |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/9/4268/pdf |doi-access=free |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011444/https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/applsci/applsci-11-04268/article_deploy/applsci-11-04268-v3.pdf?version=1620871179 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Using software that had been used to model the structures of large dams, a computer model of the dome was developed in 1980 in a collaboration between [[Enel|Italian National Agency for Electric Power]] and Structural and Hydraulic Research Centre (CRIS) by a group  of researchers led by Michele Fanelli and Gabriella Giuseppetti in cooperation with the Department of Civil Engineering of the [[University of Florence]], under the supervision of Andrea Chiarugi. Because of limited computational resources and for reasons of symmetry, only a quarter of the dome was modelled. The resulting finite elements analysis confirmed that the main cracks were essentially being created by self-weight of the dome. Since then series of numerical models of increasing complexity have been developed. To assist in monitoring of the dome an extensive photogrammetric and topographical survey of the entire dome was commissioned in 1992 by the ''Soprintendenza''. The results of this survey were then used to further develop the finite elements model of the dome.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Bartoli |first1=Gianni |last2=Betti |first2=Michele |title=The Numerical Analyses of Santa Maria del Fiore Dome: State of the Art |book-title=Proceedings of the Workshop on the Structural Cracking of the Cupola of Santa Maria del Fiore |pages=37–39 |publisher=Los Alamos National Laboratory |date=11 September 2014 |location=Los Alamos, New Mexico |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088 |conference= |access-date=3 December 2021 |archive-date=26 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220426011445/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265959088_Proceedings_of_the_Workshop_on_the_Structural_Cracking_of_the_Cupola_of_Santa_Maria_del_Fiore |url-status=live }}</ref>

'''Galata Tower''' ({{langx|tr|Galata Kulesi}}), or '''Galata Tower Museum''' ({{langx|tr|Galata Kulesi Müzesi}}), its name since it began to be used as a [[museum]], is a [[tower]] located in the [[Beyoğlu]] district of [[Istanbul]]. It takes its name from the [[Galata]] neighborhood where it stands. Built as a [[watchtower]] within the [[Walls of Galata]], the tower has served various purposes over different periods and has functioned as an exhibition venue and museum since 2020. It is one of the landmark structures of both Beyoğlu and Istanbul.

In 1267, the [[Republic of Genoa|Genoese]], who were allied with the [[Byzantine Empire]], established a [[Colonialism|colony]] called "Pera" in Galata, north of the [[Golden Horn]], and gradually expanded their sphere of control with permissions granted by the Byzantines. Known at the time as the "Tower of the Holy Cross" (Turris Sancte Crucis) because of the [[cross]] at its summit, the tower was built between 1335 and 1349 as part of the fortifications constructed in the area, after the Genoese expanded their sphere of control toward the hill to the northeast in violation of these permissions. The [[Byzantine–Genoese War (1348–1349)|war]] that broke out between the two states that year ended with a treaty signed the following year, and the hill on which the tower stood was placed under Genoese control. Following the [[Fall of Constantinople|conquest]] of [[Constantinople]] by the [[Ottoman Empire]] on 29 May 1453, the Genoese in Pera surrendered the colony to the Ottomans without resistance. Although some damage was inflicted on the fortifications in Galata, including the tower, destruction of the tower was halted by decree of Ottoman Sultan [[Mehmed II]], and the damaged sections were rebuilt. The tower, which was damaged in the [[1509 Constantinople earthquake|earthquake of 1509]], was repaired by 1510. In the 16th and 17th centuries, it was used to house prisoners of war and as a supply warehouse; from the 18th century onward, it was used as a [[fire lookout tower]] by the [[Mehter|Mehterhane corps]] and fire watchers.

Following the fire of 1794, repairs altered the tower's design, and its upper section was converted into a [[coffeehouse]]. Its design was changed once again after the fire of 1831. After its roof collapsed during a storm in 1875, two timber-framed masonry floors were added above the top floor, and this section began to be used to observe and report fires in the city. During restoration work between 1965 and 1967, the tower was arranged as a tourist attraction with floors serving different purposes, and its roof was renewed in a style resembling its design between 1832 and 1876. During this period, it was leased from the [[Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality|Istanbul Municipality]] and operated by Ünal Kardeşler and, subsequently, by a company belonging to their heirs. Its exterior underwent restoration in 1999–2000. In 2013, [[BELTUR]], affiliated with the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, took over its operation. At that time, the top two floors housed a [[café]] and a [[restaurant]], respectively. That same year, it was included on [[UNESCO]]'s [[World Heritage Sites in Turkey#Tentative List|Tentative List of World Heritage Sites]]. In 2019, ownership and operation passed to the [[Directorate General of Foundations]]. Following work carried out in 2020, the tower was converted into a museum and exhibition venue. Restoration work was undertaken on its roof in 2023.

The masonry tower, built in the [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque style]], stands 62.59 m tall to the tip of its roof. Its cylindrical shaft is made of stone. It has 11 floors, including a [[basement]], a ground floor, and a [[mezzanine]]. An elevator runs from the ground floor to the sixth floor, while stone stairs extend from the ground floor to the fourth floor and steel-structure stairs from the sixth to the eighth floor. The conical roof covering the summit is made of [[reinforced concrete]]. Today, the ground floor serves as a ticket-control and security area, and the entrance to the elevator reaching the sixth floor is also located there. The first floor houses the museum shop. The next three floors contain permanent museum and exhibition areas featuring, respectively, a simulation area with a screen showing an animation of [[Hezârfen Ahmed Çelebi]] gliding from the Galata Tower, exhibits concerning the period when the tower was used by [[Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf|Taqi al-Din]], photographs from the [[Turkish War of Independence]], information and artifacts relating to the Galata Tower and its walls, and exhibits about the Galata Tower and Istanbul. Beyond the sixth floor, which serves as a transitional area, the seventh floor is a temporary exhibition space containing a [[scale model]] depicting part of Istanbul and viewing telescopes positioned by the windows. The eighth floor is arranged as an observation terrace. The tower's exterior and the surrounding area are also used on certain special and designated days for awareness campaigns, commemorations, and celebrations.

== History ==

=== Background, construction, and the Genoese period ===
[[File:Constantinople mediaeval map.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|The Galata Tower stands at the highest point of the walls in the upper part of the map in a copy of ''Liber insularum Archipelagi'' by [[Cristoforo Buondelmonti]], dated to around the 1420s or 1430s and held at the [[Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana]].]]

In 1267, the [[Republic of Genoa|Genoese]], who were allied with the [[Byzantine Empire]], established a colony called "[[Beyoğlu|Pera]]" in [[Galata]], north of the [[Golden Horn]]. The Genoese expanded their sphere of control toward the hill northeast of the area without authorization and, between 1335 and 1349, built [[fortification]] walls and towers surrounded by [[moat]]s on the slopes of the hill. The structure now known as the Galata Tower was built in 1348. In addition to serving as a [[watchtower]], it was the principal tower of the fortifications intended to protect the colony's coastal section on the flat ground against a possible land-based siege. In front of the tower stood a [[barbican]] that projected in a semicircle from the straight line of the walls and was attached to the structure on both sides. This area, where four lines of walls converged and the main entrance to Pera was located, was the last fortification built before Pera came under the control of the [[Ottoman Empire]]. According to the plaque there, its construction was completed on 1 April 1452. During this period, the tower was known as "Turris S. [Sancte] Crucis" ("Tower of the Holy Cross"), after the [[cross]] at its summit.<ref name="Sağlam">{{journal citation |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/1461392 |title=Galata Kulesi'nin Ceneviz dönemine yönelik bir yeniden değerlendirme |first=Hasan Sercan |last=Sağlam |journal=YILLIK: Annual of Istanbul Studies |issue=2 |year=2020 |pages=53-80|access-date=6 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108080051/https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/1461392 |archive-date=8 January 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In August 1348, a [[Byzantine–Genoese War|war]] broke out between the Byzantines and the Genoese as a result of commercial disputes.<ref>{{cite book |last=Norwich |first=John |author-link=John Julius Norwich |title=A Short History of Byzantium |url=https://archive.org/details/shorthistoryofby00norw |publisher=[[Alfred A. Knopf]] |location=New York |year=1997 |language=English |isbn=9780679450887 |page=[https://archive.org/details/shorthistoryofby00norw/page/346 346]}}</ref> After the war ended in 1349 with a Byzantine victory, peace was established, and that same year a decree issued by Byzantine Emperor [[John VI Kantakouzenos|John VI]] transferred control of the hill on which the Galata Tower stood to the Genoese.<ref name="Sağlam"/>

=== Ottoman period ===
[[File:Map of Constantinople by Cristoforo Buondelmonti, Düsseldorf copy.png|thumb|left|upright=0.8|A map from a copy of ''Liber insularum Archipelagi'' dated to 1485–1490, held at the [[University and State Library Düsseldorf]].]]

Following the [[Fall of Constantinople|Ottoman conquest]] of [[Constantinople]] on 29 May 1453, the Genoese in Pera surrendered the colony to Ottoman control without resistance. During this period, the damage inflicted on the tower's summit was halted following an edict issued by Ottoman Sultan [[Mehmed II]] concerning Pera. As part of restoration work led by [[Zağanos Pasha]], the tower was raised again, and the cross at its summit was replaced with the [[Flag of the Ottoman Empire]].<ref name="Sağlam"/>

The [[1509 Constantinople earthquake|earthquake of 1509]] caused damage to the fortifications in Galata, including the Galata Tower. Repairs led by [[Mimar Hayruddin|Mimar Hayreddin]] were completed in mid-1510, and the tower was raised again.<ref name="Sağlam"/>{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=314}} Two brick bands on the tower's shaft, at heights of 13.20 m (the beginning of the second floor) and 17.17 m (the beginning of the third floor), are considered evidence of repairs made after this earthquake. Sources differ regarding the extent of these repairs.<ref name="Anadol-3">{{journal citation |url=http://dergi.mo.org.tr/dergiler/4/354/5179.pdf |title=Galata Kulesi |first=Köksal |last=Anadol |first2=Ersin |last2=Arıoğlu |pages=49-55|journal=[[Mimarlık]] |issue=158 |volume=1 |year=1979 |access-date=11 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729054304/http://dergi.mo.org.tr/dergiler/4/354/5179.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|Eyice|1969|pp=25, 36-37, 63, 75}}

In the 16th century, the Galata Tower and the other towers along the Walls of Galata were used as accommodation and a [[dungeon]] for Christian prisoners of war working at the [[Golden Horn shipyards|shipyards]] in [[Kasımpaşa, Beyoğlu|Kasımpaşa]].{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=314}} In his 17th-century work ''[[Seyahatnâme]]'', [[Evliya Çelebi]] wrote that the tower had formerly served as a dungeon and, in his time, as a supply warehouse for the shipyard.{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=314}} [[Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf|Taqi al-Din]] also carried out some work in the tower before the construction of his [[Constantinople observatory of Taqi ad-Din|observatory]].{{sfn|Eyice|1995|pp=314-315}}<ref>{{journal citation |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/13207 |title=Takiyüddin'in Pera'daki gözlemevi |first=Johannes Heinrich |last=Mordtmann |translator-first=Cem |translator-last=Pulathaneli |journal=Osmanlı Bilimi Araştırmaları |volume=10 |issue=2 |year=2009 |pages=115-129|access-date=14 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117164923/https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/13207 |archive-date=17 January 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{journal citation |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/652087 |title=Osmanlı astronomi müesseseleri |first=Salim |last=Aydüz |journal=Türkiye Araştırmaları Literatür Dergisi |volume=2 |issue=4 |year=2004 |pages=411-453|access-date=15 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121040022/https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/652087 |archive-date=21 January 2021 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{journal citation |title=Rasıd Takiyüddin'in çalışmalarında Galata Kulesinin vazifesi |first=Süheyl |last=Ünver |author-link=Süheyl Ünver |journal=Gökyüzü |publisher=[[Turkish Astronomical Society]] |volume=1 |issue=2 |year=1960 |pages=1-3}}</ref> From the 18th century onward, the tower was used as a [[fire lookout tower]] by the [[Mehter|Mehterhane corps]] and fire watchers.{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=315}}

Due to damage caused by a fire on 27 July 1794, the tower was shortened and its design altered. As part of the work, rooms projecting from each side of the uppermost floor, corridors, and a reception hall were added, and this section was converted into a [[coffeehouse]]. A [[Kus|large drum]] was installed to announce fires, while the [[attic]] was used as a [[dovecote]].{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=315}}<ref name="Anadol">{{journal citation |url=http://dergi.mo.org.tr/dergiler/2/259/3623.pdf |title=Galata Kulesinin turistik tanzimi |first=Köksal |last=Anadol |journal=[[Arkitekt]] |year=1964 |volume=4 |issue=317 |pages=150-159|access-date=19 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140720163114/http://dergi.mo.org.tr/dergiler/2/259/3623.pdf |archive-date=20 July 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref> A fire on 2–3 August 1831 caused further damage. The upper section was repaired according to an earlier design, giving the tower its present-day appearance, apart from the roof that would collapse in the storm of 1875.{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=315}}<ref name="Anadol"/>

The tower's roof was repaired in either 1853 or 1854.{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=315}} During construction of the building to be used by the [[Sixth Municipal District]], which was established in December 1857 to administer Galata and Pera, the courtyard surrounding the tower, the gates in the walls, and the sections of wall extending toward the shore began to be demolished under a decision adopted on 30 November 1863. The surrounding moats were also filled in. These works took place during the construction of the municipal building in 1864.{{sfn|Eyice|1995|pp=315-316}}<ref>{{cite book |title=İstanbul'un Tarihsel Topografyası |first=Wolfgang |last=Müller-Wiener |author-link=Wolfgang Müller-Wiener |translator-first=Ülker |translator-last=Sayın |publisher=[[Yapı Kredi Yayınları]] |edition=1st |year=2001 |page=322 |isbn=975080158X}}</ref><ref>{{journal citation |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/712007 |title=Altıncı Daire-i Belediye ve günümüz belediye hizmetleriyle karşılaştırılması |first=Şevki Bilgehan |last=Önver |journal=Takvim-i Vekayi |volume=7 |issue=1 |year=2019 |pages=37-77|issn=2148-0087 |access-date=27 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200325040001/https://dergipark.org.tr/tr/download/article-file/712007 |archive-date=25 March 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After the roof collapsed in a storm in 1875, a two-story timber structure with masonry elements was built above the top floor, with one room on each floor. The summit began to serve as a fire-reporting station for the fire brigade established in the city in 1874 and as a communications center for the [[Ottoman Navy]].{{sfn|Eyice|1995|p=316}}<ref name="Anadol-3"/><ref name="Anadol"/>{{sfn|Koçu|1971|p=5907}}
